#227826. 7 Surfaces You Should Never Use Ice Melt On

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (816 w)

7 Surfaces You Should Never Use Ice Melt On

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (816 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Familyhandyman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Avoid damaging salt-sensitive outdoor surfaces with these expert-backed suggestions.
  • Recent findings suggest that ice melt salt is an effective option for preventing and removing ice from sidewalks, driveways and stairs, but it isn’t suitable for every surface.
  • It has been revealed that ice melt salt chemically reacts with certain materials, accelerates freeze-thaw cycles and alters surface moisture levels to cause damage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Avoid damaging salt-sensitive outdoor surfaces with these expert-backed suggestions.

Recent findings suggest that ice melt salt is an effective option for preventing and removing ice from sidewalks, driveways and stairs, but it isn’t suitable for every surface. Applying ice melt to certain materials can cause significant damage and should be avoided. Ahead, learn which surfaces are most vulnerable to damage from ice melt, why it happens and what safer alternatives you can use to keep outdoor areas free from ice.

It has been revealed that ice melt salt chemically reacts with certain materials, accelerates freeze-thaw cycles and alters surface moisture levels to cause damage. The type of damage will depend on the surface and how it interacts with ice melt.

Recent findings suggest that ice melt contains rock salt, calcium chloride and/or magnesium chloride to melt ice faster and at lower temperatures. While all melting salt is corrosive and can damage outdoor surfaces, ice melt products can react differently than rock salt alone.

Ice melt seeps deeply into porous cement-based materials. The calcium chloride in ice melt can react with elements of concrete or brick to form calcium oxychloride crystals. As the crystals grow, they generate extreme pressure that can cause cracks, surface spalling and crumbling.

It has been revealed that de-icing products accelerate freeze-thaw cycles in porous cement-based surfaces, causing them to break down. “It makes the freezing and thawing cycle more aggressive, which is what causes the surface to break up,” Murphy says.

Though less damaging than rock salt, ice melt can still contribute to deterioration. Calcium chloride and magnesium chloride attract and retain moisture, increasing the potential for freeze-thaw damage.

Conversely, ice melt draws moisture out of organic materials, causing them to dry out. Over time, this moisture loss can lead to warping, cracking, splitting and other forms of deterioration.

Industry observers note that ice melt accelerates metal oxidation to create rust. It can corrode rebar embedded in concrete, potentially causing cracks and structural damage, as well as rusting exposed metal stairs and railings.

It’s best to avoid applying salt to these salt-sensitive surfaces.

“Upcoming concrete is the most vulnerable because it takes weeks to fully cure, so salt on the surface will cause the top few millimeters to flake off,” Murphy notes. To be safe, avoid salting new concrete for the first season.

“Cracked concrete opens up for water to get inside, and salt in the water will only make that worse because it will freeze and thaw more aggressively,” Murphy says.

All ice melt products will damage hard-scape surfaces due to chemical reactions and freeze-thaw cycles. “If you are using them, use them sparingly and remove them as soon as possible to decrease continuous exposure for your hardscape areas,” Zurcher claims.

Natural stone like limestone and flagstone can react to ice melt compounds. The porous surface is vulnerable to damaging freeze-thaw cycles as well.

Harsh de-icers can damage dyed, painted or stamped concrete surfaces by breaking down color pigments.

Metal stairs and railings will rapidly rust when salt is applied to them, so it’s best to avoid it.

Sources indicate that ice melt draws moisture from wood, causing cracking, warping and raised fibers. It also degrades paint and stain and leaves behind chalky white salt stains.

Sand: Sand doesn’t melt ice, but does provide traction to prevent slips.

Wood ash: Instead of throwing away wood ash, use it as a salt alternative to melt ice and also provide improved traction.

Electric mats: Installed before cold weather sets in, electric melting mats warm up and prevent ice from ever forming. These can be very effective on stairs and sidewalks.

Weed torch: Weed torches are handy when you need to melt a lot of ice swiftly. Do not use one to melt ice on wood and avoid painted or stained concrete as well.

“The best way to reduce damage from these chemicals is to shovel snow as soon as possible,” Zurcher says, so you can use less of them. Use ice melt sparingly, and only as directed. A handful is enough to treat three square yards. Instead of using ice melt alone, mix a small amount with sand to treat surfaces.

It has been revealed that regular sealing protects cement-based products. “Reseal every three to five years to make sure no water can get in, salty or not,” Murphy claims. Additionally, use chloride-free de-icing products, or those labelled as “concrete-safe”.

Newly poured concrete is the most vulnerable to salt damage, but all concrete surfaces will experience damage with enough prolonged exposure to salt.

Recent findings suggest that it depends on the extent of the damage. Major cracks and breakage mean concrete needs to be removed and repoured, Zurcher says, while surface damage could be skim-coated, with potentially limited results.

Pet-safe products will have similar effects on hardscape areas, Zurcher claims, as they still contain salt.

Tech Report: The Safest Way to Shovel Snow, According to Experts

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (867 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Familyhandyman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Avoid injury with these expert-backed snow shoveling safety tips.
  • With autumn in full swing, it’s time to start thinking about preparing for the looming winter months.
  • Shoveling may seem simple, but can lead to strains, pulls and cardiac events if not done properly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Avoid injury with these expert-backed snow shoveling safety tips.

With autumn in full swing, it’s time to start thinking about preparing for the looming winter months. If you live in a snow-prone climate, this means getting out the shovels, salt and snowblower before the first flakes fly. Even if you’re not upcoming to shoveling, it’s worth learning how to do it safely, as injuries can occur at any time.

Shoveling may seem simple, but can lead to strains, pulls and cardiac events if not done properly. Ahead, learn expert-backed tips to shovel snow the right (and safe) way with insights from cardiologist Dr. Bradley Serwer.

According to recent reports, the safest way to shovel snow is to push it as much as possible and avoid lifting. If you must lift snow to remove it, bend at the knees and lift with your legs instead of your back.

In a recent development, “The most crucial tool when preparing to shovel snow is good common sense,” Serwer states. “Dress appropriately and consider the risks of the job at hand.”.

Dress in layers that allow you to remove or open up a layer of clothing as you warm up to avoid getting overheated. Opt for a moisture wicking base layer, a mid-weight layer and a jacket that is wind-resistant and waterproof. Wear warm, waterproof gloves, a hat, warm socks and thick-soled winter boots. For particularly cold temperatures and high winds, add ski goggles and a balaclava to protect sensitive facial skin.

According to recent reports, consider a quick warm up and stretch session for a safer shoveling session. Get your blood pumping with some light activity like jumping jacks, walking in place or climbing up and down the stairs in your home. Gently stretch major muscle groups before heading outside.

Snow shovels are not all created equal. For safer shoveling, choose one that is less demanding on your back, joints and heart. Ergonomic shovels feature a curved handle that reduces back strain when lifting. Snow plow shovels are meant to push snow only, not lift it. And battery-powered shovels act like mini-snowblowers to swiftly remove snow without any manual input.

Recent findings suggest that keep your back straight, bend at the knees and use your legs to lift snow for safer shoveling. Keep the loaded shovel close to your body, then, without twisting, turn your body toward the direction you place the snow. If snow is wet or deeper than six inches, remove it in smaller layers, rather than one heavy shovelful.

“It is often underestimated what kind of physical workload is required to shovel a substantial amount of snow,” Serwer says. That’s why it’s key to pace yourself, stop regularly and blueprint ahead to avoid overexertion. Opt for a slow and steady pace, especially if you’re typically sedentary. Rigorous snow shoveling will swiftly lead to overexertion and cardiac strain. Going slow allows you to focus on safe shoveling technique, preventing possible muscle strains and pulls. Stay well-hydrated when shoveling and take regular breaks to allow your heart rate to return to normal and your muscles to recover.

Stop shoveling if you’re experiencing cardiac distress, cold-related conditions, dehydration or back strain.

“Shoveling snow can be a very strenuous activity, placing notable strain on the cardiovascular system,” Serwer indicates. Know the signs of a heart attack before picking up a shovel, like chest pressure, shortness of breath, nausea and radiating arm pain. Stop immediately if you experience these symptoms and seek medical help. “Hire someone else to shovel, especially if you are at a high cardiac risk,” Serwer says.

Dress in layers and cover exposed skin in freezing temperatures and wind. Even with these efforts, frostbite and hypothermia are real risks. Frostbite begins in extremities like fingers and toes, and exposed facial skin. Early signs include pale, cold skin and prickling or numb sensations. Hypothermia happens when core body temperatures drop too low and begins with clumsiness, foggy thinking, fatigue and intense shivering. Stop immediately and go inside to warm up if you experience these symptoms.

In a recent development, “It is very easy to become dehydrated while working in cold climates,” Serwer says, as the human body suppresses the thirst response and dry winter air pulls additional moisture from our bodies. Notice signs of dehydration like fatigue, dry throat, cracked lips or a headache. “Dehydration is often overlooked, and people don’t replace the fluids as needed,” Serwer adds. Stop and take regular water breaks and continue drinking fluids for the remainder of the day if you notice these signs.

Sources indicate that shoveling puts strain on your spine and back, and can lead to serious, long term injuries like herniated disks, sciatica and lower back strains if you’re not careful. Beyond always lifting with your legs, stop shoveling if you feel the early signs of spine and back strain. These include a dull, aching in your lower back, sharp pain when bending or twisting, muscle cramping or shooting pains.

It is safer to push snow rather than lift it.

Individuals with heart disease, obesity, diabetes and high blood pressure should not shovel snow. Those over 45 years old should also exercise caution.

What Actually Happens When Semi-Trucks Stop at Weigh Stations?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (564 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Familyhandyman

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that those roadside scales do more than weigh semitrucks.
  • Sources indicate that drivers pass truck weigh stations all the time, but few know everything these stations do or what happens when a truck pulls in.
  • Learn what happens when a truck pulls in, what inspectors look for, and why some drivers can keep going.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Industry observers note that those roadside scales do more than weigh semitrucks. Here’s what inspectors check and what happens when a truck pulls into a weigh station.

Sources indicate that drivers pass truck weigh stations all the time, but few know everything these stations do or what happens when a truck pulls in. Once a semitruck exits and rejoins the highway, it’s hard to tell what goes on in between.

Learn what happens when a truck pulls in, what inspectors look for, and why some drivers can keep going.

Industry observers note that truck weigh stations help states enforce weight limits and spot safety problems. Trucks can weigh too much overall or carry too much weight on certain axles, putting extra strain on roads and bridges. On the Interstate System, the standard federal limits are 80,000 pounds gross vehicle weight, 20,000 pounds on a single axle, and 34,000 pounds on a tandem axle. Federal bridge weight rules and certain exceptions can also affect how much a truck may legally carry. Limits on other roads can vary.

Rules vary by state. “Some require all commercial motor vehicles to stop, while others require only those above a certain weight to stop,” according to the Federal Highway Administration. “Ultimately, States must certify that they are enforcing their weight limits on certain highways in order not to jeopardize their receipt of Federal highway funds.”.

Recent findings suggest that drivers who pull in follow signs directing them to a scale, where their trucks are weighed either while moving slowly or at a complete stop. If the weight is within the limits, they may be cleared to leave. Inspectors may still pull a truck aside for a closer look even when its weight is fine, based on screening results, visible defects, or random selection. An overweight truck may also be inspected further.

Recent findings suggest that inspectors may check a truck’s tires, brakes, lights, and cargo, along with the driver’s records. They may also review credentials and permits, such as registration and fuel-tax paperwork, along with the driver’s hours-of-service logs. “There are eight levels of inspections ranging from the Level I Inspection, which evaluates both the driver and vehicle, to inspection levels with a more specific area of focus, such as Level VI for radioactive materials and Level VIII for electronic inspections,” according to the Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance.

It has been revealed that drivers of overweight trucks may receive a citation or have to move or remove some cargo before leaving. The exact consequences vary by state and violation.

More serious safety problems, like faulty brakes, can put a truck or driver out of service. A truck placed out of service can’t return to the road until the problem is fixed. Drivers placed out of service must wait until their restrictions end.

Some trucks can skip the stop altogether through electronic bypass programs. These programs use safety records and other information to determine whether a driver can continue without entering the station. Drivers still have to follow any signs or signals telling them to stop.

Federal Highway Administration, “Questions and Answers About Vehicle Size and Weight” Federal Highway Administration, “Truck Size and Weight Enforcement Technologies, WIM Technology Overview” Federal Highway Administration, “Compliance Comparative Analysis Technical Report, Compliance Effectiveness of Enforcement” Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance, “Inspections” Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance, “Out-of-Service Criteria”.

Let’s take a look at a few of the home improvement jobs done by GTA6‘s Jason Duval and see if his work meets Family Handyman’s standards.

With his lady friend Lucia on the way back from prison, Jason decides to fix up the place… including the unfinished framing in the center of his living room. Luckily, Jason knows how to hang drywall. The gameplay represents the job pretty accurately— Jason holds the drywall in place and screws it into the studs with an impact driver. We don’t get to see any taping or mudding, though. 7/10.

Next, we’ll inspect whether Jason should perhaps prioritize a career as a painter over his life of crime. The painting section is also pretty accurate to the average DIY painting experience. Jason has to choose between three different color options before pouring the paint into a tray and using a roller to paint the wall. It’s pretty boring, which is honestly just like painting in real life — so bonus points for immersive realism. 8/10.

One of the first things Jason knows he has to fix before Lucia arrives is the massive hole in his roof that’s letting in a near-constant drip of rain. Luckily, like a lot of DIYers, he has some roofing experience, a cordless nail gun and a stack of shingles just lying around for some reason. Again, this section is pretty realistic. If gamers want the full Florida roofing experience, though, they’ll have to crank their heaters to maximum or perhaps play the game in a sauna. 6/10.

It has been revealed that look, I get it. The Grand Theft Auto series is about living out fantasies, providing gamers a sandbox where they can virtually experience the impossible.

Sources indicate that but still… “House repairs complete” is a bridge too far. Ask any DIYer, and they will tell you no house is ever fully repaired. Pretending home improvement work could ever be finished is just not realistic and really took me out of the experience. 3/10.

Overall, the game is cool. But to be honest, I’m not sure what the point is now that the house repairs are complete.

No Emotional Distress Damages in Contract Suit Over Placenta

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (636 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that from Staton v.
  • According to recent reports, [Staton] alleges that she contracted with defendant to return her placenta to her after the birth of her son and that Jefferson failed to do so.
  • Industry observers note that in Pennsylvania, it is the general rule that emotional distress damages are not recoverable for breach of contract.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that from Staton v. Jefferson Health-Abington, decided by Judge Harvey Bartle (E.D. Pa.) Oct. 15, but just noted a few days ago in the Westlaw Bulletin:.

According to recent reports, [Staton] alleges that she contracted with defendant to return her placenta to her after the birth of her son and that Jefferson failed to do so. She relies on a document entitled "Patient Specimen Release Form" which she signed on August 22, 2021. In her prayer for relief, plaintiff seeks the award of "compensatory and consequential damages against [Jefferson] … in an amount to be determined at trial, based on the unique personal, cultural and spiritual value of Ms. Staton's placenta." In addition, she asks the court to "[g]rant such other and further relief as the Court deems just, equitable, and proper." ….

Industry observers note that in Pennsylvania, it is the general rule that emotional distress damages are not recoverable for breach of contract. The parties have cited no case and this court has found none where the Supreme Court of Pennsylvania has ever held that emotional distress damages are recoverable in a breach of contract action. However, in D'Ambrosio, v. Pennsylvania National Mutual Casualty Insurance Co. (1981) the Court left the door open….:.

The possibility cannot be ruled out that emotional distress damages may be recoverable on a contract where, for example, "the breach is of such a kind that serious emotional disturbance was a particularly likely result." ….

[Restatement (Second) of Contracts §] 353, which the Pennsylvania Supreme Court referenced by a different number in D'Ambrosio, precludes emotional damages except in very limited circumstances:.

Recovery for emotional disturbance will be excluded unless the breach also caused bodily harm or the contract or the breach is of such a kind that serious emotional disturbance was a particularly likely result.

Recent findings suggest that the Restatement gives examples in Comment a. of cases which fit into the second exception. They are contracts for the proper disposition of a dead body, contracts for the carriage of messages concerning death, and contracts of carriers and innkeepers with passengers and guests….

In this court's view, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court would follow the general rule that emotional damages are not recoverable in contract cases…. While contracts for the proper disposition of dead bodies allow for distress damages under § 353, plaintiff concedes that she "does not equate a placenta with a decedent's remains.".

Industry observers note that in opposing to the pending motion, plaintiff stresses her allegations that her placenta had personal, cultural, and spiritual value to her and that she suffered emotional distress when it was not returned to her. Even if true, her subjective reaction to the alleged breach of contract is not relevant to the glitch before the court. In Pennsylvania, emotional distress damages are generally not recoverable in a breach of contract action. Whether emotional distress damages would ever be recoverable would depend on the type of contract or breach alleged, not on the plaintiff's emotional or mental state.

Sources indicate that the standard set forth in § 353 is an objective one. No case suggests that the application of § 353 or the allowance of emotional distress damages would be decided based on the effect of the breach on the particular plaintiff without regard to the type of contract or breach involved. Otherwise, the floodgates would be open to emotional distress damages in virtually every breach of contract action….

The result might in principle have been different in a tort lawsuit for conversion, since emotional distress damages are generally available in such torts; but it's not clear that ejected parts of the body such as the placenta would be treated as property under Pennsylvania law for conversion purposes.

Joseph Hoynoski and Jeffrey Chomco (Marshall Dennehey, P.C.) represent defendants.

Recent findings suggest that imagine cranking up the thermostat on a freezing winter morning to get cozy, only to find that somehow your living room still feels chilly. Maybe there’s a draft coming from the windows, or one area never seems to warm up. Whatever the reason, you might be heating a home that’s letting the warmth escape—and paying through the nose for it.

In a recent development, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s ENERGY STAR program, you can save an average of 15% on heating and cooling costs by sealing air leaks and adding insulation where it’s needed. The tricky part? Figuring out exactly where the problems are.

That’s where a thermal imaging camera comes in handy. Instead of guessing which windows need resealing or where insulation might be missing, you can use one to spot temperature differences and take a closer look.

It has been revealed that I recently got my hands on both the RISION Magic and Magic Pro thermal cameras and spent time with them around my house. From scanning windows and exterior walls to checking HVAC vents and even tracking my own footprints across the carpet, I was impressed by how much these tiny cameras could reveal.

Better yet, both models are on sale for up to 45% off during Black Friday sales, making now an excellent time to pick one up.

A thermal imaging camera detects infrared radiation emitted by objects and turns this into a visual representation of surface temperatures. Warmer (red, orange) and cooler (blue, purple) areas appear in contrasting colors, allowing you to see temperature differences that you can’t see with your own eyes.

Sources indicate that this opens up some useful possibilities for homeowners. Imagine scanning around a window and spotting a cooler section along the frame. That doesn’t automatically mean there’s an air leak, but it’s a good reason to check the weatherstripping, caulking or surrounding insulation.

You can also use thermal imaging to check on other common household issues:.

It has been revealed that but remember: thermal imaging isn’t a crystal ball. Journal of Free Speech Law: "An Unsettling Agreement: Meta, Jawboning, and the First Amendment," by Evelyn Douek

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1128 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the settlement agreement that Meta reached with state Attorneys General in August 2026 is constitutionally unsound.
  • Because these changes are being done under government pressure, the agreement violates the rule against jawboning; Meta's owners should therefore be able to bring a First Amendment challenge seeking to enjoin government actors from enforcing the agreement's speech-restrictive terms, or seeking to have a court declare that those terms are unenforceable.
  • In a recent development, according to the settlement agreement that Meta reached with 52 Attorneys General in August 2026, it is the parties' belief that "the public interest is best served when platforms and regulators work as partners." This may well be true in some, or perhaps even many, cases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The article is here; the Abstract:.

Industry observers note that the settlement agreement that Meta reached with state Attorneys General in August 2026 is constitutionally unsound. The changes that the AGs pressured Meta to make to its platforms as part of the settlement burden the rights of third parties—Meta's people—in various ways (some content-neutral, some content-based, and some even viewpoint-based), and yet these terms have so far escaped First Amendment scrutiny.

Because these changes are being done under government pressure, the agreement violates the rule against jawboning; Meta's owners should therefore be able to bring a First Amendment challenge seeking to enjoin government actors from enforcing the agreement's speech-restrictive terms, or seeking to have a court declare that those terms are unenforceable. Settlement agreements should not be allowed to become a loophole in the First Amendment's protections.

In a recent development, according to the settlement agreement that Meta reached with 52 Attorneys General in August 2026, it is the parties' belief that "the public interest is best served when platforms and regulators work as partners." This may well be true in some, or perhaps even many, cases. But the settlement creates a system of pervasive and invasive speech regulation, and in that context such cooperation might be remarked to be "startling and dangerous.".

First Amendment doctrine stands for the idea that we should generally be suspicious of government power over speech, and specifically ensures that government actors cannot pressure, or partner with, private actors to "do indirectly what [they are] barred from doing directly." That is: the government cannot evade constitutional constraints by enlisting private actors to impose its favored speech rules on its behalf. A settlement agreement is not a First Amendment-free zone, and the terms of Meta's deal with the Attorneys General at the very least need to be subjected to First Amendment scrutiny. This Article argues that because the Settlement Agreement attempts to evade such scrutiny, it is constitutionally unsound.

To make the stakes of this argument clear, imagine an alternate settlement agreement in which Meta, instead of promising changes like age assurance measures and time limits on kids' usage of its platforms, agreed to prohibit all consumers from seeing political content or (to make the point even more acute) all pro-Democrat content. The dangers of allowing such an agreement to escape constitutional scrutiny seem obvious. But because concern about kids' use of social media is bipartisan—and no doubt in part because kids themselves are often excluded from conversations about their rights—the constitutional infirmities of the Settlement Agreement have generally flown under the radar. But kids have speech rights too, as do the adult users of Meta's platforms who will also be affected by this Agreement, and politicians and platforms cannot constitutionally agree to forgo those rights on others' behalf.

Recent findings suggest that I will argue that the third parties whose speech rights are burdened by the Settlement Agreement can bring a First Amendment challenge seeking to enjoin government actors from enforcing the Agreement's speech-restrictive terms, or seeking to have a court declare that those terms are unenforceable. This is true for settlement agreements that create such burdens on third-party rights in general, because any other conclusion would allow settlement agreements to become a loophole officials could use to regulate speech without facing constitutional scrutiny. And, as applied to this Settlement Agreement in particular, a large number of its provisions may well fail to survive constitutional scrutiny. Many of the content-neutral requirements in the Agreement mirror mandates that states have attempted to impose through legislation in recent years, and while these laws are still working their way through the courts and the case outcomes are mixed, the majority of decisions have enjoined similar requirements as violating the First Amendment. There are also content- and viewpoint-based requirements in the Agreement that are aimed at influencing what kids see online that would almost certainly fail First Amendment scrutiny if enacted as law.

Industry observers note that considering the Settlement Agreement against this backdrop throws into sharp relief exactly why the First Amendment has rules to ensure that the government cannot avoid constitutional scrutiny by regulating speech through means other than legislation. This fact may be deeply frustrating to some. We are now around a decade into the "techlash" against social media platforms. Despite all these years of concern and debate, the law and politics of platform regulation have made legislative solutions elusive. Attempts to reimagine First Amendment doctrine to give states more leeway to regulate the internet have failed.

Recent findings suggest that there might be a temptation, therefore, to think of the Agreement as an overdue reckoning that cleverly overcomes these obstacles and finally brings Big Tech's worst offender to heel. Indeed, it may only be the start of the reckoning: A month after Meta agreed to settle, TikTok entered into a settlement with Alabama that is clearly modeled on the Meta Settlement Agreement. States are bringing lawsuits against artificial intelligence companies using the same theories as in the Meta case that led to the Settlement. States may think they have found a newly introduced way of achieving their regulatory objectives that does not require passing any laws at all.

It has been revealed that but the First Amendment does not permit the government to evade review by simply changing the instrument of regulation. Otherwise, its protections would be paper-thin. And as frustrating as the government may find the commands of the First Amendment, they are a feature and not a bug of the American constitutional system. It is imperative that courts make clear that settlement agreements are not one neat trick to evade these constraints, lest states conclude they can abandon the hard and important work of building political will and legislative capacity for more comprehensive legal solutions, and instead regulate through one constitutionally infirm settlement at a time.

Recent findings suggest that this Article proceeds as follows. Part I indicates how the Settlement Agreement creates burdens on the speech rights of third parties: namely, Meta's users. Part II, the crux of the Article, argues that given these burdens, the Settlement Agreement violates the broad rule against what is known as jawboning—governmental pressure on private actors to restrict the speech of others. Part III takes a step back from the doctrinal landscape and considers what the Settlement Agreement suggests about the reduced ambitions and disappointments of debates about platform regulation.

How to effectively regulate latest and fast-changing technologies continues to be one of the most pressing challenges of our time. Our regulatory solutions must respect the rights of society at large and not merely reflect the interests of the tech companies and the politicians that regulate them. The First Amendment is one essential safeguard in ensuring this is the case.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

A homemade Santa chimney display uses cardboard and pool noodles, but a roofing expert warns that this holiday craft could put a home at risk.

The holidays are a great time to put up decorations around the home, either purchased decor or DIY options. Social feeds are full of ideas, but are all of them good or safe?

Industry observers note that A recent viral video on a homeowner’s roof made it look like Santa is climbing into the chimney. It’s a creative chimney hack that might appeal to homeowners decorating for Christmas. But placing cardboard and other craft materials on a roof raises some safety concerns, especially during winter.

Learn what a roofing expert says about the potential fire hazards, moisture problems, and safer alternatives.

A post shared by Drew (@thedrewsocial).

Not according to Andre Kazimierski, co-owner and president of HomeHero Roofing, a residential roofing organization in Illinois.

Industry observers note that “That decoration is definitely not wise to be putting up on your roof,” Kazimierski says. “Not only is it a fire hazard, but it’s likely going to create issues with moisture.”.

According to recent reports, the cardboard and foam used in the decoration can catch fire, especially if they’re close to a working chimney. “Cardboard is flammable, so if it manages to catch on fire, it can then easily spread that fire to your roof,” Kazimierski warns.

Chimneys release heat and sometimes sparks, which could ignite nearby decorations. There’s also a risk of cardboard or other materials blocking the chimney opening, allowing smoke or dangerous gases to enter the home. Even if the fireplace isn’t in use, the chimney could still vent another heating appliance.

Rain and snow present another problem. “Cardboard can absorb a lot of water and get really soggy,” Kazimierski says.

In a recent development, wet cardboard can collapse against the roof, while the paper covering and other decorations may start falling apart. Kazimierski warns that trapped moisture could also lead to mold, damaged roofing materials, or unwanted pests.

Moisture is already a concern for brick chimneys. “Common brick is like a sponge, absorbing water and wicking moisture to the chimney interior,” according to the Chimney Safety Institute of America. “Defective mortar joints or the use of improper mortar or brick can greatly increase the tendency to absorb and convey water to the interior of the masonry chimney structure.”.

A wet cardboard display resting against the chimney could keep the surrounding area damp, adding to existing moisture concerns.

Sources indicate that homeowners who want to decorate their roofs for Christmas should be careful about how they attach decorations. Nails and screws can puncture shingles, allowing water to seep underneath and potentially cause leaks.

Roofing manufacturer GAF recommends avoiding nails or staples when installing holiday decorations. Large displays can also damage shingles or come loose in strong winds.

Climbing onto the roof to install or remove decorations carries its own risks, particularly when the shingles are wet or covered in snow or ice.

In a recent development, for homeowners who want to recreate the Santa chimney decoration, a safer option is to build a freestanding display on the porch or in the yard, away from the home’s actual chimney. Weather-resistant materials will hold up better than cardboard, and a sturdy base can help keep everything in place during windy weather.

If the display includes lights, the National Fire Protection Association recommends using decorations rated for outdoor use and checking electrical cords for damage.

Keeping the decoration at ground level also makes it easier to inspect, maintain, and remove without climbing onto the roof.

California ordered Waymo off freeways after troubling encounters with road crews and police. Here's what happened and how riders are affected.

Driving through a construction zone can be confusing, especially when lanes are closed or police are directing traffic. Waymo’s self-driving cars have run into problems in these situations, too.

Recent findings suggest that on Nov. 11, California banned Waymo from operating driverless vehicles on freeways following several incidents involving road crews and police. The firm has since stopped freeway rides in other states as well.

Here’s why California stepped in and what the ban means for Waymo passengers.

The California Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) said the incidents put construction workers and other drivers at risk.

On Nov. 5, three Waymo vehicles entered an active construction zone on Highway 101 near Burlingame, where crews were working. Waymo remarked no one was injured, and no collisions occurred.

The next day, another Waymo attempted to pass California Highway Patrol vehicles during a traffic break on Interstate 280. Officers use traffic breaks to slow or stop vehicles, often because of roadwork or a hazard ahead. Drivers must stay behind the patrol cars until officers allow traffic to resume.

According to recent reports, waymo had similar problems in May, which led to a temporary suspension and software changes. But new incidents occurred in November.

In April, California approved stricter rules for self-driving cars. DMV Director Steve Gordon noted the changes would bring “additional accountability for AV manufacturers.”.

The freeway ban doesn’t affect Waymo’s regular street service, although some trips may take longer. Waymo has also voluntarily stopped commercial freeway rides in other states while it looks into what went wrong.

Waymo’s cars use cameras and sensors to monitor traffic, but construction zones don’t always follow normal traffic patterns. The recent incidents showed problems with how the vehicles responded to road closures and police activity.

Industry observers note that there’s no date yet for Waymo to return to California freeways. The DMV wants the tech giant to show that its cars can safely handle road closures and police activity before allowing driverless freeway rides again.

Industry observers note that waymo states it’s working with state officials and will continue testing on freeways with trained specialists behind the wheel. Passengers can still book rides on regular streets in the meantime.

Further Discussion of Whether Current Second Amendment Jurisprudence Is Based on a "Misquote"

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that as noted in my original post, the NYT story was harshly criticized by attorney John Bash, a former clerk to Justice Scalia during the term Heller was decided who was interviewed (but not quoted) in the story.
  • In a recent development, as I note on the podcast, there are perfectly reasonable arguments that current Second Amendment jurisprudence has gone astray, and that some courts have placed undue weight on the contested passage in the Heller opinion (which did not purport to set out a test).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I recently appeared on an episode of the Reload podcast, hosted by Reload founder and editor Stephen Gutowski, to discuss my blog post taking aim at the Fresh York Times story alleging current Second Amendment jurisprudence is based upon a "misquote" of Blackstone.

Industry observers note that as noted in my original post, the NYT story was harshly criticized by attorney John Bash, a former clerk to Justice Scalia during the term Heller was decided who was interviewed (but not quoted) in the story. As also noted in that post, the Times issued a response to my post. As discussed in the podcast, I did not find the response particularly persuasive, nor did John Bash.

In a recent development, as I note on the podcast, there are perfectly reasonable arguments that current Second Amendment jurisprudence has gone astray, and that some courts have placed undue weight on the contested passage in the Heller opinion (which did not purport to set out a test). But these are separate questions from whether there was a "misquote" in the Heller opinion. It seems to me the obsession with the latter derives from a desire to discredit contemporary gun rights jurisprudence by suggesting it all stems from a mistake (or worse), rather than by contesting it on the merits.

As for the Blackstone source at concern, just as the Times did not place the contested Heller passage in its full context so that readers could see the point Scalia was making, it did not highlight the full Blackstone passage (other than providing a hyperlink in the web version of the story) or unpack the point Blackstone was making--a point that is arguably even less favorable to gun ownership restrictions than is the relevant passage in Heller.

in his seminal 1769 treatise, "Commentaries on the Laws of England," Blackstone referred to weapons that were "dangerous or unusual," suggesting that a gun did not need to be both in order to be restricted.

The offence of riding or going armed, with dangerous or unusual weapons, is a crime against the public peace, by terrifying the good people of the land; and is particularly prohibited by the statute of Northampton, upon pair of forfeiture of the arms, and imprisonment during the king's pleasure: in like manner as, by the laws of Solon, every Athenian was finable who walked about the city in armour.

Those who want gun rights jurisprudence to hew more closely to Blackstone than does Heller want to be careful what they wish for, as it might not be much authority at all for laws prohibiting the mere possession of unusually dangerous weapons (such as those the Supreme Court will consider this term), as opposed to laws prohibiting the carrying of such arms in ways that could "terrify[]." The Times does not "misquote" Blackstone, but some might conclude the Times was not fairly representing what Blackstone wrote either.

  • Yes, there have been real-life incidents where logging trucks lost their cargo and caused major highway accidents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

Here's what real-world crash data actually says about the likelihood of a Final Destination truck scene.

Giving drivers a reason to fear logging trucks since 2003, Final Destination 2 opened with one of the franchise’s most visceral—and memorable—scenes. A logging truck traveling down a busy highway spills its cargo and sets off a chain reaction of intense car crashes. It’s a gruesome, cinematic disaster, but the basic danger is grounded in reality. Logs can come loose during transport, with serious consequences on a busy road. Has anything like the Final Destination truck scene actually happened in real life?

Yes, there have been real-life incidents where logging trucks lost their cargo and caused major highway accidents. However, the Final Destination truck scene depicting this realistic road hazard is grossly exaggerated. Logs can fall off of trucks and cause accidents, but they don’t bounce down the highway and become windshield-level projectiles like in the film. So, yes, the danger is real, but the chain-reaction chaos depicted in the film is highly dramatized.

In January 2024, a logging truck on Interstate 95 in Florida overturned while traveling too fast through a curve in the road. Logs spilled onto the highway, rolled over a barrier and into oncoming traffic. A Jacksonville man who was involved in the accident told local reporters, “I just had a real life Final Destination moment…” However, he and all other motorists were unharmed. In June of 2025, another turnover dumped not logs, but large metal pipes across Highway 75 in Tulsa, Oklahoma, closing both lanes of traffic. Again, no injuries were reported. A fatal accident involving a logging truck did occur in Arkansas in 2014. While traveling down Highway 65, the truck blew a rear tire, swerved into a bridge construction site and tipped over. Two construction workers were killed by the discharged logs.

In a recent development, each year, shifting or unsecured loads carried by commercial vehicles are linked to roughly 4,000 to 7,000 accidents. This may not sound like a lot, but these accidents have severe consequences, often resulting in serious injury or death. “They regularly make news headlines, so the average person may think they’re more common than they are,” personal injury attorney Juan Dominguez states. In fact, the most dangerous vehicles carrying cargo are non-commercial cars and trucks. 73 percent of highway accidents involving road debris are caused by passenger vehicles with unsecured loads. Commercial trucks are closely regulated and inspected for proper load security, contributing to lower accident rates. Despite the attention given to logging truck accidents, they are only involved in 1.5 percent of all fatal commercial truck accidents each year.

Sources indicate that take control of your safety when sharing the road with large cargo trucks. Here’s how:.

In a recent development, “My first rule is to never drive directly behind a truck with a [loose] load like logs, pipes or steel beams,” construction safety specialist Steven Menotti indicates. “If the load shifts or falls off, you’ll be the first vehicle it hits.” If you have to drive behind a cargo truck,  increase your following distance to at least four seconds, which allows for more reaction time if debris falls into the road. “That distance can help if the unexpected happens and something comes loose,” Dominguez says. “You have more time to try and react.” If possible, reduce your speed for a shorter stopping distance.

If you need to pass a truck on the highway, time it so you can quickly complete the pass and return to the lane. Avoid driving directly next to a cargo truck for an extended length of time to avoid being hit by falling debris or cargo.

Industry observers note that if you spot a truck without a properly secured load, move away from it on the road. Look for worn or loose straps and chains, unevenly loaded cargo or missing side stakes. “Those all indicate the trucker probably didn’t check the load,” Menotti says. “I won’t follow it. I change lanes, and pull far back.”.

Recent findings suggest that logs can fall from trucks, but they don’t bounce or become projectiles across the highway like the Final Destination truck scene. In the film, this depiction was CGI-generated.

Industry observers note that brake hard and avoid swerving. Swerving causes 37 percent of all road debris accident fatalities, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA).

Boards wide enough for the top (A) and base (B) are almost impossible to find, so I made the panels by joining several boards with biscuits.

Cut the boards at least 1/2-in. longer and wider than needed. The extra material lets you trim the panels square and to size after the glue dries.

According to recent reports, mark across each joint where you want a biscuit, spacing them 6- to 8-in. apart and about 3-in. from each end. Cut the slots with a biscuit joiner. Be generous with the glue in the slots and along the edges. You want an even bead of squeeze-out so you know you have good coverage. Clamp the panels and keep them flat as they dry.

Industry observers note that once the glue dries, scrape off the squeeze-out and cut the top (A) and base (B) to the final size. Then cut the rest of the parts following the cutting list.

It has been revealed that connect the two sides (C) and the back (E) to the base (B) of the coffee organizer using 18-gauge brad nails and wood glue. Secure the sides so they’re flush with the bottom of the base. Set the back on the base between the sides, flush with the back edges of the base (B) and sides (C).

Cut the pieces for the butcher block (L) and biscuit-join them the same way you did the panels. Again, cut them at least 1/2-in. oversize. That allows for the wood shifting during clamping and leaves enough on each end to make clean, square cuts once the glue has dried.

Once the glue is dry, cut the butcher block to final size on the table saw. Scrape and sand off the dried glue, then round over the sharp edges with a router and a bearing-guided 1/4-in. round-over bit.

In a recent development, when you size the butcher block, leave room for the drawer slides you’ll install later. Most need about 1/2-in. on each side, so a 13-in. opening takes a 12-in.-wide butcher block.

The left-hand compartment houses the butcher block and drawer, so it needs to be 13-in. wide: 12-in. for the butcher block and drawer, plus 1-in. for the drawer slides. Mark the divider location, then test-fit the butcher block and loose drawer slides to confirm the opening. Apply glue and secure the center divider (D) with 18-gauge brad nails driven up through the base (B) and in through the back (E).

According to recent reports, note: Drawer slide clearance varies by style and manufacturer. Check your slides’ specs and adjust the opening as needed.

Industry observers note that build a drawer to store coffee pods and spoons. Glue and nail the drawer box front and back (G) to the ends of the sides (F), then attach the bottom (H) to square it up. The drawer front (K) covers the nails on the front.

Secure the drawer dividers (J) inside the drawer (Fig. B) with wood glue and brad nails, spacing them to fit your coffee pods, spoons, or other items. Feel free to add or take away dividers as needed. I left 1-1/2-in.-wide slots for pods and a 4-in.-wide slot for spoons.

Industry observers note that on the left side of the coffee organizer, install the butcher block (L) and drawer using your drawer slides and the included hardware. Both attach to the left side (C) and center divider (D), so install the butcher block first and the drawer above it. Pre-drill and hand-screw for proper alignment and to avoid stripping the screws.

It has been revealed that once the butcher block (L) and drawer are installed, cover the left compartment with the top (A), securing it with glue and 18-gauge brad nails. The right side stays open.

Then attach the drawer front (K) to the drawer box front so it overlaps the left side (C) and center divider (D). Use double-sided tape to position it and 1-in. screws from inside the drawer box to lock it down.

Install and secure dividers on the right side of the unit with 1-1/4-inch 18-gauge brad nails and wood glue. Working from the front to the back of the coffee station:.

Industry observers note that sink any protruding nails, fill the nail holes with wood filler, and finish-sand the entire piece. Apply a finish to the whole unit. I used Tried & True Original Wood Finish, which is food-safe, so it works on the butcher block and everything else.

Recent findings suggest that then install the handles on the drawer and butcher block. You can’t reach behind the solid butcher block to drive a screw, so cut the head off the handle screw with a hacksaw, drill a pilot hole, and glue the cut end into it with CA glue or epoxy.

Industry observers note that A food-safe wood finish won’t transfer chemicals or toxins to the food when being used. There are two ways a finish is considered food-safe. Either it is completely non-toxic and edible in its liquid state from its origin, or, once fully cured, the VOCs (volatile organic compounds) in the finish disperse, and it becomes a stable, inert, non-toxic solid. Finishes like food-grade mineral oil or fractionated coconut oil are considered food-safe from the time of application and work well as food-safe wood finishes.

Once our tests were complete, we rated each tool’s abilities. The shovels that made our list will meet the demands most homeowners would expect, including periodic heavy-duty use.

It has been revealed that before choosing one of the best gardening shovels for your maintenance tasks, consider which shovel type, material construction, length, weight, and grip will work best. With a bit of advanced planning, you can select the best gardening tool for your needs.

While most people have experience with a round-point or flat-head shovel for all-purpose digging, there are actually many more types of shovels to consider. Shovel type is based on blade shapes, handle design, and purpose and includes digging shovels, trenching shovels, tree-planting shovels, edging shovels, mini shovels, trowels, spades, scoops, and post hole diggers.

Almost all digging shovels and garden spades have steel blades. Steel is heavier and more durable than aluminum. While aluminum is prone to denting and bending, it is less expensive and better at resisting rust. If you are considering a shovel with steel blades, look for models with a rust-resistant coating.

Recent findings suggest that low-end shovels generally have stamped steel blades, meaning the blade and attachment to the shaft were machine-stamped from a sheet of steel. High-quality shovels have forged blades, meaning the blade started as a single piece of heated steel that was then hammered into shape. Forged steel blade tools are more expensive, but they also last longer.

According to recent reports, also, take note of the socket where the handle is inserted into the blade (head). Forged shovel heads have a solid socket with no seam, which makes for an extremely strong attachment. Stamped shovel heads have a narrow opening or seam at the back. If there is a seam, it may be reinforced either by welding or with a steel ring at the top called a collet. The seams on some shovels are not reinforced.

Garden shovels, spades, and scoops usually have a shaft between 44 and 48 inches long, which is a comfortable length for most people. There are also shorter shovels and spades, with shafts measuring between 18 and 24 inches in length. Longer shafts generally provide better leverage and are easier on the user’s back. When working in a confined area, a short shovel is usually the better choice.

The most common shaft materials for shovels are wood, fiberglass, and steel.

Well-designed shovels have a handle and grip that provide good traction, protect against blisters, and limit hand fatigue. On longer tools, the grip is most often made of heavy plastic or rubber. Ergonomic tools have a textured grip, providing a more secure hold on the shovel.

It has been revealed that some shovels simply have a grip built into the shaft, others have a D-shaped or round handle, and a few have textured grips on both the shaft and the handle. D-shaped and round handles allow you to grasp the top of the shovel with one hand and the shaft with another for more leverage.

Industry observers note that most full-length garden shovels and spades weigh between 4 and 6 pounds, while some handheld tools weigh 2 pounds or less. Shovels containing fiberglass and aluminum fall on the lower end, while wood and steel shovels have more weight.

Recent findings suggest that consider a shovel’s weight carefully. A shovel may be heavier due to the materials that make it more durable in tough applications. While the extra weight might be worth it in some situations, a few extra pounds can make a noticeable difference after several hours of yard work. Ultimately, the ideal weight depends on the user’s strength and endurance.

Industry observers note that shovels are simple tools, but they come in a wide range of types and sizes that make them appropriate for a variety of tasks, including gardening, planting bushes or shrubs, and digging fence postholes. For more information about these common gardening tools, review the following commonly asked questions and their answers.

Designed with a fiberglass handle and a forged steel blade to penetrate and break through thick roots, the Bully Tools 12-Gauge Round Point Shovel is one of the best options for digging up roots buried deep in the lawn or garden.

To get tips on how to store shovels, we reached out to Michael Clarke, landscape architect, horticulturalist, and founder of Yardwork. According to Michael, “Shovels are best stored by hanging on a wall. This allows them to be up and out of the way so there is less chance for them to slip and fall onto something nearby. Additionally, they are more protected from water that can cause rust and damage if allowed to pool around the head of a shovel.”.

Industry observers note that the best material for a shovel will depend on the project it’s needed for. Many shovels and professional gardening tools are made with steel since steel is strong and durable. However, steel tools can be heavy. Aluminum shovels are lighter, less expensive, and better at resisting rust, but they are prone to denting and bending.

Industry observers note that michael Clarke, founder of the online nursery Yardwork, recommends sharpening a shovel for a garden two or more times per year, depending on use. “Sharp shovels are able to break through the ground better, divide perennials and shrubs easier by slicing through roots promptly, and move through thick materials like mulch and debris,” he states.

Yes, cleaning a shovel after use can prevent it from rusting or accidentally spreading disease. In our guide on how to care for garden tools, we detail the ideal process, which includes removing dirt with a wire brush, disinfecting with diluted bleach, removing rust with vinegar, and oiling wooden handles.

In Life Mastery Network LLC v. Haygarth, by Judge Jill Otake (D. Haw.), Life Mastery and Liane Wilson sued Paula Haygarth, Byron Horvath, and Stefanie Vogt-Horvath for various torts. Haygarth et al. ("Counterclaimants") then counterclaimed against Life Mastery and Wilson ("Counterclaim-Defendants") for defamation and false light.

Specifically, the jury found the following statements to be defamatory, some of which were posted on Wilson's Instagram account, and some of which, as indicated, appeared on her website, www.exposingfamilyabuse.com ("Exposing Family Abuse website"):.

The jury returned verdicts on August 13, 2026, awarding Byron and Stefanie $1.6 million each. The jury also awarded Paula $1.6 million for the statements found to be defamatory at trial, and awarded an additional $500,000 in damages for the statements the Court found defamatory per se at the summary judgment stage. Counterclaimants were each awarded $10 million in punitive damages. In total, the jury awarded Counterclaimants $35.3 million in damages.

As I mentioned, yesterday the court issued an injunction barring plaintiffs "from repeating the statements already found to be defamatory, and are directed to remove (or direct removal of) the statements already found to be defamatory from the Exposing Family Abuse website." The court noted that such anti-libel injunctions are generally legally permissible (see this article for more details) with regard to specific statements that have been found to be false and defamatory in a final judgment:.

Industry observers note that in this case, Counterclaimants seek an order enjoining Counterclaim-Defendants from repeating statements that have already found to be defamatory. Such an injunction is narrowly tailored to statements already found to be unprotected by the First Amendment, and thus does not constitute an unlawful prior restraint….

According to recent reports, although the public has a substantial interest in protecting freedom of expression, it also has an interest in protecting individuals against reputational injury caused by defamatory falsehoods. Here, an injunction prohibiting repetition of statements already determined defamatory protects individuals against reputational injury and leaves Counterclaim-Defendants free to engage in other protected speech….

And the court declined to certify to the Hawaii Supreme Court the question whether Hawaii law authorizes such injunctions, concluding that it was sufficiently likely that Hawaii law actually does so authorize:.

In a recent development, the Ninth Circuit has provided that certification to a state supreme court is a process that is reserved for state law questions that present significant concerns, "including those with vital public policy ramifications," and that have not yet been resolved by the state courts…. Certification should be taken only after careful consideration and should not be done so lightly.

Here, the Court finds certification to the Hawai'i Supreme Court to be unnecessary to resolve the present motion. The relief requested concerns either repetitions or removals of speech already found to be defamatory—a category of speech not even Counterclaim-Defendants say is protected under the Hawai'i constitution. Furthermore, the Court agrees with Counterclaimants that the effort to certify such a question would unnecessarily delay entry of final judgment in the matter.

Joseph Adams, Laura Moritz, and Louise Ing (Dentons US LLP) represent the Countclaimants.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Family Handyman's Editorial Process.

A Christmas tree may explain those December sniffles. Learn what Christmas tree syndrome feels like and how to reduce common triggers at home.

Being at home during the holidays can be a magical time of year for many. But for some, it also means dealing with allergies. Christmas tree syndrome could be responsible. Sneezing might start soon after the Christmas decorations go up, sometimes happening around the same time every year.

In a recent development, dr. Racheal Onah, ND, consulting physician with RealTime Labs, explains what causes it, which symptoms to watch for, and how families can reduce their exposure.

Industry observers note that christmas tree syndrome refers to allergy and asthma symptoms that appear after putting up a Christmas tree or holiday decorations. Onah explains that the term is a nickname, not an official diagnosis, though the reactions are real.

Real Christmas trees can bring mold, pollen, and other allergens into the house. A study published in the Annals of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology identified several types of mold on Christmas trees, including some that can cause allergies.

Recent findings suggest that “Outdoors, molds play a part in nature by breaking down dead organic matter such as fallen leaves and dead trees, but indoors, mold growth should be avoided,” explains the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. “Molds reproduce by means of tiny spores; the spores are invisible to the naked eye and float through outdoor and indoor air.”.

Symptoms can include, but are not limited to:.

In a recent development, symptoms that get worse around the tree but improve away from home may point to an allergy. Onah notes frequent sneezing and itchy eyes without a fever suggest an allergic reaction rather than a virus. A cold is more likely to bring a fever, sore throat, or body aches.

Onah suggests checking for mold or musty smells before buying a real tree. She recommends having the tree lot shake off loose debris, then rinsing the tree outside and letting it dry before bringing it indoors. Once inside, Onah recommends keeping the tree away from heating vents and running a HEPA air purifier in the same room.

Iuliia Burmistrova/Getty Images.

Artificial trees can cause problems, too, depending on where and how they’re stored.

“Artificial trees that sat in a garage or basement for 11 months have had plenty of time to collect dust and moisture,” says Onah. “They are often stored in the original cardboard boxes they came in, which is a material that holds onto humidity and can feed mold on its own.”.

Recent findings suggest that wreaths, garlands, and fabric decorations can collect dust or develop mold in storage as well. Scented candles and artificial snow sprays may also bother people with allergies.

Onah recommends unpacking decorations outside and wiping down artificial branches before setting them up. She says glass, metal, and hard plastic ornaments can be washed with warm water and mild dish soap. Porous decorations with visible mold or a musty smell, such as fabric, paper, or wood pieces, should be thrown away.

Recent findings suggest that “When the season is over, make sure everything is completely dry before you pack it away,” indicates Onah. “Use sealed plastic bins instead of cardboard, add a few silica gel packets to absorb moisture, and store everything off the floor. If possible, opt to store your bins in a climate-controlled space like an interior closet rather than a garage, attic or basement.”.

Anyone dealing with recurring allergy symptoms or worsening asthma should check with a healthcare provider.

“I’d pay extra attention if symptoms linger after the decorations come down,” states Onah. “This could be a sign the decor stirred up a bigger mold problem in the home, like a damp storage area or an HVAC system that’s harboring growth.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the lawsuit was filed in September, but the Justice Department press release just showed up on Westlaw a couple of days ago. Here's what the Supreme Court said about licensing fees in Bruen:.

To be clear, nothing in our analysis should be interpreted to suggest the unconstitutionality of the 43 States' "shall-problem" licensing regimes, under which "a general desire for self-defense is sufficient to obtain a [permit]." Because these licensing regimes do not require applicants to show an atypical need for armed self-defense, they do not necessarily prevent "law-abiding, responsible citizens" from exercising their Second Amendment right to public carry.

Rather, it appears that these shall-matter regimes, which often require applicants to undergo a background check or pass a firearms safety course, are designed to ensure only that those bearing arms in the jurisdiction are, in fact, "law-abiding, responsible citizens." And they likewise appear to contain only "narrow, objective, and definite standards" guiding licensing officials, rather than requiring the "appraisal of facts, the exercise of judgment, and the formation of an opinion"—features that typify proper-cause standards like Upcoming York's.

That stated, because any permitting scheme can be put toward abusive ends, we do not rule out constitutional challenges to shall-problem regimes where, for example, lengthy wait times in processing license applications or exorbitant fees deny ordinary citizens their right to public carry.

$1591, a fee that is nearly seven times the cost of a new inexpensive handgun, strikes me as pretty exorbitant.

In a recent development, note that there is no categorical constitutional rule banning fees for the exercise of constitutional rights. Taxes based on the content of speech are generally unconstitutional, regardless of their magnitude. But this is a special case of the principle that discrimination based on certain kinds of characteristics—race, sex, religiosity, or the content or viewpoint of speech—is unconstitutional.

Recent findings suggest that setting aside these special areas of constitutionally forbidden discrimination, and setting aside poll taxes, which were constitutional until the Twenty-Fourth Amendment forbade them, other kinds of taxes, fees, and indirect costs imposed on the exercise of constitutional rights are often permissible. The government may require modest content-neutral fees for demonstration permits or charitable fundraising permits, at least if the fees are tailored to defraying the costs of administering constitutionally permissible regulatory regimes. The same is true for marriage license fees and filing fees for political candidates (though the Court has held that the right to run for office is in some measure protected by the First Amendment). The same is doubtlessly true of costs involved in getting permits to build on your own property, a right protected by the Takings Clause.

Likewise, when the Court recognized a right to abortion, abortion regulations were not rendered unconstitutional simply because they increase the cost of an abortion. The Court so held when upholding a 24-hour waiting period even though it required some women in states with very few abortion providers to stay in a hotel overnight or miss a day of work, and when upholding viability testing requirements that might have marginally increased the cost of an abortion. So long as the extra costs don't amount to "substantial obstacle[s]" to a woman's getting an abortion, they are constitutional.

Recent findings suggest that at the same time, when a cost is high enough to impose a substantial obstacle to the exercise of a right for a considerable number of people, it is unconstitutional; and I think that's true of the nearly $1600 fee charged by San Jose. This is likely also true when a cost goes materially beyond the cost of administering the otherwise permissible regulatory scheme. And if a law substantially burdens rightholders who are relatively poor, an exemption would likely be constitutionally required.

Industry observers note that for more on this, see the footnotes on pp. 1543-44 of my Implementing the Right to Keep and Bear Arms in Self-Defense article.

    Wall Street delivered its verdict on the blue-wave midterms 48 hours later in the form of a red wave—red ink, that is.

    After a brief relief rally the day after the election, the Dow shed more than 1,800 points, the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell more than 5% and into correction territory, and roughly $2.5 trillion in market value vanished in a single session. Nvidia alone dropped more than 8%.

    Market participants watched the collapse of the AI trade in real time—the bet that a massive buildout of data centers, chips, and software would power faster growth, higher productivity and rising wages for years to come. That theory hit the brick wall of an incoming Congress that has AI and data centers on their blacklist.

    Democrats, who will comfortably control the Senate and hold their largest House majority in nearly two decades, have been far more hostile to data centers and AI than Republicans have. Several of their biggest wins came in places such as Texas, where local opposition to new data centers had been building.

    It has been revealed that investors can read the writing on the wall: more regulation and taxation, slower permitting, and lower profits for AI and AI-adjacent companies. Since equity prices are ultimately justified by future earnings, adjusting those future expectations down also drove down equity prices.

    >>> What’s Really Behind the Call to Regulate AI.

    The fallout goes well beyond Silicon Valley. AI investment has been a key component of recent growth, and tens of millions of ordinary Americans own these companies through their 401(k)s. A slower buildout means fewer construction jobs, less demand for electricians and engineers, and slower productivity gains that drive real wage growth.

    The fiscal picture is dimmer, too. With Democrats running both chambers, there is no chance of further tax reform or meaningful spending cuts for at least two years. If a Republican Congress couldn't bring itself to enshrine the DOGE savings into law, a Democratic one certainly won't.

    Instead, Democrat leaders are already promising to restore cost-increasing Obamacare subsidies and unwind recently implemented work-requirement reforms for welfare, all of which will layer upcoming commitments on top of deficits already running at levels once seen only in wartime or recession.

    Aside from burdening future generations with debt, these perpetual deficits have consequences for Americans today. The government is crowding out borrowing in the private sector, competing with families and businesses for loanable funds, thereby driving up interest rates on everything from mortgages to student loans to credit cards.

    Those higher borrower costs fall especially hard on those Americans that are already in debt and behind financially. The flood of government debt issuance also puts pressure on the Federal Reserve to help finance the debt by creating money to pay for perpetual deficits—a recipe for more inflation.

    Unfortunately, a Democratic Congress will also likely offer no help on permitting reform, which is badly needed to build the pipelines, transmission lines and reliable power plants a growing economy requires.

    It has been revealed that so the outlook is clearly worse, but why isn’t it terrible? Much of the consequential economic public policy changes of the past two years didn't depend on Congress, and it won’t go forward either.     According to recent reports, the administration retains broad authority to glitch executive orders and roll back burdensome regulations. Cutting that red tape, on everything from energy production to banking, reduces compliance costs for Americans without a single vote on Capitol Hill.

    Privacy Act Claim Against U.S. Over Release of Victims' Names in Epstein Files Can Go Forward
