    Tech Report: Philippines: As ICC Tries Duterte, Stalled Justice at Home

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3205 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that (Manila) – Philippine authorities have failed to investigate extrajudicial killings in the “war on drugs” since former President Rodrigo Duterte was transferred to the International Criminal Court for prosecution, Human Rights Watch stated today.
    • President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who took office in June 2022, pledged to pursue prosecutions of Duterte-era “drug war” killings and established a Justice Department task force for the purpose, but only four cases have reached the courts.
    • Industry observers note that “President Marcos’ pledge to hold police accountable for past and ongoing abuses in its anti-drug campaign has been a failure,” said Lian Buan, Southeast Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that (Manila) – Philippine authorities have failed to investigate extrajudicial killings in the “war on drugs” since former President Rodrigo Duterte was transferred to the International Criminal Court for prosecution, Human Rights Watch stated today. The ICC trial in The Hague against Duterte for crimes against humanity is scheduled to begin on November 30, 2026.

    President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who took office in June 2022, pledged to pursue prosecutions of Duterte-era “drug war” killings and established a Justice Department task force for the purpose, but only four cases have reached the courts. Families of victims seeking to file newly introduced cases face significant barriers. Meanwhile, government records and human rights group reports show that drug-war abuses continue, with police harassing, arbitrarily arresting, and at times killing suspected drug dealers and users.

    Industry observers note that “President Marcos’ pledge to hold police accountable for past and ongoing abuses in its anti-drug campaign has been a failure,” said Lian Buan, Southeast Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch. “The Philippine government needs to prioritize justice for all drug-war victims and provide their families’ adequate redress.”.

    Recent findings suggest that between September and November 2026, Human Rights Watch interviewed 13 people, including 7 drug-war victims and their families both under Duterte and Marcos, 4 human rights defenders, and 2 government officials; reviewed recent data and reporting on drug-related killings; and analyzed a database of local government Peace and Order and Public Safety Plans. Human Rights Watch also requested and received information from the Philippine Justice Department and Commission on Human Rights on drug-war cases before the courts.

    Recent findings suggest that relatives of drug-war victims described a justice system in which the burden of uncovering evidence of an unlawful killing fell mostly on them instead of government prosecutors. “It’s so hard to prove that you’re telling the truth,” said a woman whose husband was killed in 2016 in a police “buy-bust” drug sting operation. “It’s tiring pursuing a case here—it’s as if we can never pass the tests.”.

    Recent findings suggest that some facing obstacles to justice have pinned their hopes on the ICC. “In the Philippines, what was our chance, given how the government works,” stated another woman whose husband was killed by unidentified assailants in 2016. “In the ICC they are impartial, that’s where our hope is.”.

    During the Duterte presidency from 2016 to 2022, the Philippine National Police reported 6,200 deaths during anti-drug operations, although United Nations agencies, the Philippine Commission on Human Rights, the Supreme Court, and domestic human rights groups put the number of killings by police and unidentified assailants at between 20,000 and 30,000.

    In a recent development, only five cases of Duterte-era “drug war” killings, involving nine police officers, have resulted in convictions. Government prosecutors initiated the first three cases, following the successive murders of three teenage boys in Caloocan in August 2017, which sparked public outrage. The fourth and fifth cases—for killings in 2016—were filed through the efforts of nongovernmental legal groups and led to convictions in 2024 and 2025.

    In November 2024, the Justice Department created a task force to investigate and prosecute extrajudicial killings during Duterte’s “war on drugs” but only four cases it identified have advanced to trial, with three others under preliminary investigation, based on Justice Department data.

    According to recent reports, the Marcos administration, after arresting and surrendering Duterte to the ICC in March 2025, announced renewed efforts to advance domestic accountability for the “drug war.” But families and human rights groups who met with Justice Department officials remarked that they were concerned the government’s witness protection program would not keep their families safe if they pursued charges against police officers. Meetings between victims’ groups and the Justice Department tapered off.

    Recent findings suggest that duterte will stand trial at the ICC for three counts of crimes against humanity of murder and attempted murder allegedly committed when he was mayor of Davao City, and then president between November 2011 and March 2019. The prosecution’s case focuses on a non-exhaustive list of 56 specific incidents and 87 victims, while noting that “[its] evidence demonstrates that the attack [against a civilian population] was broader than this representative sample of incidents.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the ICC is a court of last resort, only stepping in when domestic authorities are unwilling or unable to investigate and prosecute crimes under its jurisdiction. In November 2021, the Duterte government asked the ICC prosecutor to defer his investigation, opened in September 2021, claiming that national authorities had begun their own drug-war investigations of extrajudicial killings.

    Industry observers note that in January 2023, ICC judges ruled that the Philippine government had failed to demonstrate that it took sufficient action to investigate and prosecute Duterte-era killings and authorized the resumption of the ICC prosecutor’s investigation. The decision was upheld on appeal.

    The ICC trial against Duterte begins as the court is under growing pressure from the US government, which has vowed to dismantle the ICC “brick by brick.” On October 9, the Trump administration sanctioned the ICC, escalating its attack on the court and adding to existing sanctions on ICC judges and prosecutors, three Palestinian groups, and a UN human rights expert. The Trump administration sanctions reaffirm the ICC’s critical role as a court of last resort, Human Rights Watch stated.

    Recent findings suggest that marcos has never repudiated the “war on drugs” as a government policy and has yet to rescind the orders and other policy statements Duterte issued that underpinned the anti-drug campaign. In its review of a database of 2023-2025 local government budgets, Human Rights Watch found that 77 municipalities had allocated funds for anti-drug campaign awards and rewards, or for financial support to informants, police officials, and other local officials. Two of those municipalities, and another eight municipalities specifically referred to “neutralization” or “negation” of suspects; terms used as euphemisms for “killing” in 2016 police circular that set out the “war on drugs.” While such incentives are not necessarily unlawful, those linked to enforcement goals or operational results can create pressure to meet targets and encourage abusive practices, including extrajudicial killings.

    In a recent development, despite a significant decline in drug-related extrajudicial killings during the Marcos administration, such killings and other abuses continue, particularly in low-income urban areas where they remain routine. As of November 7, there have been at least 1,342 public reports of drug-related killings under Marcos, according to the independent monitoring of the Dahas project. These reports identified uniformed officers as responsible for 486 of those deaths.

    The Philippine government’s failure to hold those responsible to account perpetuates a climate of impunity. Families of drug-war victims under the Marcos administration encounter many of the same past obstacles when seeking justice, but the Justice Department has no task force or special mechanism to investigate post-Duterte cases, Human Rights Watch mentioned.

    Sources indicate that “Even if killings are down from the ghastly Duterte years, President Marcos’ pledged ‘bloodless campaign’ against drugs has been anything but bloodless,” Buan noted. “To end these abuses, Marcos needs to stop the brutal ‘drug war’ and put in place a robust and impartial law enforcement and judicial system.”Elusive Justice for Killings during Duterte and Marcos Administrations.

    Sources indicate that under the Duterte administration in 2020, the Justice Department opened an inter-agency panel to “reinvestigate” drug-war killings by the police. The panel identified 52 cases in which the Philippine National Police carried out internalinvestigations. However, by 2024, when Marcos was in office, the panel had only filed six cases in court. In November 2024, the Justice Department created a newly introduced task force on Duterte-era drug war killings. It began investigations anew and worked mainly with the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI)—the Justice Department’s investigative arm—instead of with the police to avoid conflicts of interest when developing cases implicating police officers.

    In a recent development, despite renewed Justice Department efforts, victims’ families still struggled to file charges. Many victims’ families who wanted to pursue charges could not do so because their relative’s death certificate declared an illness as the cause of death, even though they were found with gunshot wounds to their heads and bodies. During the height of Duterte’s “drug war,” police pressured families to sign waivers stating that they did not want to conduct autopsies or pursue charges, in exchange for faster retrievals of the bodies from funeral homes. Many families could not afford the autopsy fees, and without accurate government death records, they could not pursue charges.

    The woman whose husband was killed in a police operation in 2016 decided in 2022 to retrieve documents about his killing from the police because she believed the climate of fear had lifted under Marcos. “They were not really helping us,” she remarked. “They just left us there to search their logbooks.” Police officials had named the woman’s husband as a drug suspect killed in an “armed encounter” in a news report that featured her children wailing for their dead father. Yet she never found a police report of the operation, only a record of bystanders injured. She was unable to prove he was shot dead, because his death certificate lists the cause of death as pneumonia and his body was cremated. Government investigators have not pursued a case. The woman recalled the one conversation with the Justice Department: “They said, ‘If you have no document like police report or autopsy, it’s hard to file a case.’ So, what about me? I had no documents.”.

    The woman whose husband was killed by unidentified assailants did not know for years the circumstances under which her husband was killed. She found his body with gunshot wounds at a funeral home in 2016 and signed a waiver not to conduct an autopsy. His death certificate listed pneumonia as cause of death. After Marcos became president, the woman sought help from a nonprofit law group. In 2023, she had her husband’s body exhumed and examined by a forensic pathologist, Raquel Fortun. The autopsy highlighted that he died from gunshot wounds to the head.

    In a recent development, that year, she finally found the police report from the night her husband died. It stated that police responding to reports of gunshots found him dead with three sachets of crystal meth, and a piece of cardboard that read “I’m a drug pusher, don’t be like me.” She had an interview with the NBI, who told her they had also summoned local officials and the funeral home. But nothing further happened in the investigation. “No one has followed up with me, I still wonder what happened to that NBI case,” she said.

    Sources indicate that fortun became a commissioner of the Philippine Truth Commission, a civil society initiative working closely with the Catholic Church to investigate Duterte-era drug war crimes. She has recorded 13 cases in which people were shot and killed but whose death certificates cite illnesses such as heart attack, pneumonia, and high blood pressure as causes of death. Fortun said during a Truth Commission briefing that government prosecutors have pushed back when presented with evidence of falsified death certificates in court. In one case, the government prosecutor acted on behalf of the defendant, instead of the victim: “I was grilled in cross-examination, and I was surprised that it was the prosecutor. I don’t understand it. So if you’re a poor family with a similar case, would you still have it corrected. It’s so hard.”.

    The Commission on Human Rights told Human Rights Watch that its investigations of Duterte-era drug-war killings have resulted in cases moving through the justice system. Between 2016 and 2023, 25 cases were filed in court, 37 cases at the Office of the Ombudsman, and 42 with the Justice Department. No further progress was reported by the commission on the cases filed. The commission has no prosecutorial power and can only file cases in a manner similar to private complainants.

    Despite the Commission on Human Right’s limited powers, families seek confirmation from the commission that they have been victims of rights violations, which entitles them to limited financial assistance under the commission’s internal rules of procedure. Yet the commission denied assistance for lack of evidence to two women whose husbands were fatally shot in 2016.

    Only the woman who exhumed her husband’s body was able to challenge the decision; after she submitted the postmortem examination report in August 2026, the commission told her to file a petition for reinvestigation. “I just want to prove that what I’m saying is the truth,” she said.

    The commission told Human Rights Watch that it created its own task force, which is currently reinvestigating 493 cases of Duterte-era drug-war killings, with the goal of resolving 140 before the end of 2026.

    Duterte-Era Drug-War Policy Persists.

    Industry observers note that the mother of a man killed by police in Central Luzon in 2022—after Marcos became president—mentioned that she tried to pursue murder charges. She cited a witness who told her that her son was lured to the location the night of the killing, and an autopsy report that indicated he had been shot execution-style and not during an armed encounter as police had claimed. The witness has since gone missing. Prosecutors dismissed her case twice, most recently in 2025, because a medical expert’s testimony was required. The mother said that she was working on finding a medical expert to testify, but even just the cost of reproducing copies of documents was weighing on her.

    Recent findings suggest that no special task force has been created to investigate alleged drug-war crimes under the Marcos government. The government has claimed that its anti-drug campaign is “bloodless” and that “rather than resorting to violence, it focuses on strengthening prevention and rehabilitation efforts.” But Human Rights Watch found that disturbing Duterte-era language, such as “neutralization,” remains in prepares for current anti-drugs campaigns.

    There is no legal definition of “neutralization,” but on July 1, 2016, Duterte’s police chief, Ronald Dela Rosa, issued Command Memorandum Circular 16-2016, the operational document for the anti-drug campaign, instructing police officers to “neutralize” suspected criminals.

    In a recent development, in 2017, two human rights groups, the Center for International Law (CenterLaw) and the Free Legal Assistance Group (FLAG), filed petitions before the Supreme Court seeking to declare the anti-drug campaign unconstitutional, citing the use of the word “neutralization” in the circular. The Supreme Court has yet to rule on the case. ICC prosecutors have accused Duterte of developing “a State policy to ‘neutralize’ through violent crimes, including murder, alleged criminals in the Philippines who were perceived or alleged to be involved in drug-related and other crimes,” noting the language in the circular.

    Recent findings suggest that in November 2025, the ICC issued a sealed arrest warrant for Dela Rosa. He is alleged to be responsible for the crime against humanity of murder as part of a common initiative together with other co-perpetrators—including Duterte—with the aim of killing drug suspects between 2011 and 2019. This included issuing the Command Memorandum Circular 16-2016, instructing police officers to “neutralize” suspected criminals. The ICC unsealed the warrant in May 2026; Dela Rosa has since gone into hiding.

    The Marcos government has not rescinded that circular, but in 2024 the Philippine National Police told lawmakers that they were actually following a new circular without the word “neutralize.” The Marcos government also committed todrug policy reform as part of a US$4 million joint human rights program with the United Nations.

    Recent findings suggest that A 2026 study by two organizations, No Box Philippines and Harm Reduction International, found that the Philippine government was still allocating millions of US dollars for local anti-drug campaigns whose policy documents retained similar language to the original circular, such as “neutralization” and “negation.” Their findings were based on an analysis of 2023-2025 local government “Peace and Order and Public Safety” budgets. Local governments are supervised by the Department of Interior and Local Government, the executive department that also supervises the police.

    Human Rights Watch analyzed local government plans obtained by the two groups, and found that 85 towns, municipalities, and cities allocated funds for rewards, awards, and incentives for successful anti-drug operations, including 10 municipalities where the funds were specifically for “conducting negation operations” or “neutralizing drug personalities.”.

    During the Duterte presidency, for an area to declare itself “drug-free,” local councils had to monitor, surveil, and compile a drug “watch list.” Human rights groups frequently alleged the lists determined who would be killed, whether the assailants were police officers or masked police agents.

    Under public safety plans in effect under Marcos, local governments still offer financial rewards for making their areas “drug-free,” by giving “incentives to assets,” or “awards/rewards for significant illegal drugs accomplishment” or “neutralization of drug personalities.” ICC prosecutors alleged in their case against Duterte that “law enforcement personnel knew that extrajudicial killings would result in them being financially rewarded.” There have been fewer drug-related killings under Marcos, but human rights defenders who live in drug-war hotspots in Metro Manila and neighboring provinces remarked abuses continued.

    According to recent reports, “Their raids are not as brazen, but they still plant evidence,” one rights defender said. The quota system—the number of arrests and kills under Duterte to qualify for rewards—“was still alive.”.

    Under Marcos, human rights defenders monitoring drug-war abuses in their communities have observed that the police are more likely to extort victims than to kill them, targeting many of the same people who were on drug “watch lists.” They said police still arbitrarily arrest people, threaten them with drug charges, and then detain them on criminal anti-street-gambling charges with lighter penalties. The Philippine organization PhilRights has documented that “police officers offer to cover the victims’ release costs in exchange for repayment with interest, effectively profiting from the arrest.”.

    In 2025, a man came home one night to find police officers in the vicinity, his sister said. “They patted him down and found nothing,” she said. “But a police informant handed sachets of crystal meth and forced him to admit it was his.” The police arrested the man and took his bicycle. She said she made several visits to the police station where her brother had been detained. The police officials told her he had been charged with gambling. “I told them, ‘You said you found drugs, now the charge is gambling. How long are you detaining him?’” she said. “They told us we can ‘just pay P10,000 [$160].’ But we had no money at all at the time.”.

    Industry observers note that the sister took a month processing documents in several police stations before her brother was released. He was detained for a month without being brought before a judge in violation of his rights. “We can still see them surveilling our area from time to time,” the sister said.

    This publication has been updated to attribute the source of the data for drug-related killings under the Marcos administration.

    Philippine Police Killings in Duterte’s “War on Drugs”.

    16 Days of Activism Against Gender-Based Violence

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (434 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Every year during the 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence women’s rights defenders come together to remember women facing violence—including those we have lost—and to renew the struggle for gender equality.
    • This year we face growing gender inequality, as the rights of women and girls are rolled back and threatened by authoritarianism and conflict in many countries.
    • In the United States and Russia, authorities are dismantling reproductive rights.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Every year during the 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence women’s rights defenders come together to remember women facing violence—including those we have lost—and to renew the struggle for gender equality.

    This year we face growing gender inequality, as the rights of women and girls are rolled back and threatened by authoritarianism and conflict in many countries. Across all regions, governments and powerful anti-rights movements seek to dismantle hard-won rights for women and girls. Technology is adding new dimensions to abuse, from online harassment and surveillance to digitally enabled threats, violence, and sexualized deepfake images;  women politicians are often targeted.

    In the United States and Russia, authorities are dismantling reproductive rights. In Africa, lawmakers, with support from foreign conservative groups, are promoting a charter aiming to roll back women’s rights across the continent. In Argentina, funding for preventing GBV has been scrapped.

    According to recent reports, as armed conflict increases across the globe, more women and girls are living in proximity to fighting. During conflict, women and girls face heightened risks of sexual and gender-based violence, displacement, and economic insecurity, often with little access to protection or justice. In Sudan and Democratic Republic of Congo, sexual violence is a common feature of ongoing conflict with survivors facing significant barriers to obtaining protection, services, and justice. In Myanmar, women political prisoners are tortured. Reproductive rights are a casualty of Israel’s closures in the West Bank, its ongoing blockade of the Gaza Strip, and its continued attacks on Palestinian health facilities.

    But activists refuse to accept erosion of women’s rights.

    In March, the Commission on the Status of Women called for strengthening access to justice for all women and girls. In April, the European Parliament passed a resolution calling for consent to be the determining factor in rape legislation across the EU. In November, Hungary declared it would ratify the Istanbul Convention, strengthening women’s rights protections. Activists from Afghanistan are fighting to have gender apartheid recognized as an international crime.

    Industry observers note that activists are also pushing back against technology-facilitated abuse, demanding that companies protect, rather than endanger, women and girls. In different countries young women are leading protest movements to challenge corruption and authoritarianism.

    Rights defenders will not lose hope.

    Violence Against Lesbian, Bisexual, and Queer Women and Non-Binary People.

    Hong Kong: Fire Anniversary Underscores Growing Repression

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (766 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (London) – The Hong Kong government should ensure meaningful accountability for the devastating fire that killed 168 people one year ago and end its suppression of peaceful criticism, Human Rights Watch stated today.
    • On November 26, 2025, Hong Kong’s deadliest fire in decades engulfed seven residential high-rise buildings at Wang Fuk Court, Tai Po.
    • It has been revealed that “The Hong Kong government responded to the horrific Wang Fuk Court fire by using Beijing’s tactics of shutting out the voices of the victims and promising an elusive accountability,” noted Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (London) – The Hong Kong government should ensure meaningful accountability for the devastating fire that killed 168 people one year ago and end its suppression of peaceful criticism, Human Rights Watch stated today.

    On November 26, 2025, Hong Kong’s deadliest fire in decades engulfed seven residential high-rise buildings at Wang Fuk Court, Tai Po. The authorities initiated an independent investigation and arrested three dozen people implicated in crimes. The Housing Minister resigned. But the authorities have also threatened and arbitrarily arrested those engaging in criticism and activism concerning the fire.

    It has been revealed that “The Hong Kong government responded to the horrific Wang Fuk Court fire by using Beijing’s tactics of shutting out the voices of the victims and promising an elusive accountability,” noted Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “The authorities need to recognize that the only way to prevent similar tragedies in the future is to allow people to speak out safely and hold those responsible fully accountable.”.

    The authorities have engaged in apparent acts of repression of free expression in the weeks ahead of the anniversary:.

    Police Commissioner Joe Chow mentioned police routinely asked organizers about upcoming public events, while decisions on whether to proceed “rested with the organizers themselves.”.

    Amid continued restrictions on freedom of expression and peaceful assembly in Hong Kong, Hong Kong communities around the world have planned commemorations of the fire.

    In a recent development, deep concerns surrounding the 2026 anniversary follow a year-long government crackdown on criticism, reporting, and civil society-organizing related to the fire. Immediately following the fire, hundreds of people gathered near Wang Fuk Court to donate and distribute supplies to victims, but as the volunteer effort grew, police told them to leave and government workers took over the site.

    Authorities targeted people calling for accountability. Just four days after the fire, national security police reportedly arrested a university student, Miles Kwan, for “seditious intent” after he initiated an online petition calling for an independent investigation into the fire, and two others on suspicion of “inciting hatred against the government.”.

    Hong Kong and Beijing authorities subsequently accused “foreign forces” and “anti-China destabilizing forces” of using the fire to “incite hatred against the government.” Within hours of these announcements, two prominent online commentators, Ellie Yuen and Hailey Cheng, who had been frequently quoted in foreign media, said they would stop reporting on the fire.

    National security police also arrested the online commentator Wong On-yin in December after he planned to hold a news conference about the Wang Fuk Court fire and discussed on YouTube his subsequent questioning by police. The authorities prosecuted him for allegedly obstructing a national security investigation and publishing “seditious material.” He remains in custody awaiting a verdict in January 2027.

    Between April and May 2026, the authorities barred Wang Fuk Court residents from displaying banners from their homes or being accompanied by journalists as they were briefly permitted to return to their apartments to retrieve belongings.

    Recent findings suggest that also in May, the authorities arrested the former Wang Fuk Court owners’ committee member Kong Cheung-fat and his wife on allegations of fraud and money laundering. Kong had joined other owners in seeking a meeting to discuss insurance and other post-fire complications. While out on bail, he noted he would no longer give interviews or comment publicly. Some residents said his arrest made them more cautious about speaking publicly.

    In a recent development, an independent committee, set up by Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee, published a report on October 29 that found wide-ranging regulatory failures across four government bodies, including inadequate oversight of renovation work and fire safety, weaknesses in building maintenance regulation, and supervisory failures by contractors and other professionals. That day, Lee and senior officials formally apologized to the victims of the fire and their families while promising to implement “systemic reforms.” Housing Secretary Winnie Ho later stepped down from office while the authorities arrested 35 people in connection with the fire and possible corruption in the renovation project.

    “An apology and promises of reform are no substitute for ensuring that people can freely question and criticize the authorities,” Pearson said. “The Hong Kong government should act on the independent committee’s recommendations and provide adequate compensation and other support for victims and their families.”.

    Academic Freedom in Hong Kong Under the National Security Law.

    • A recent New York City law banning horse-drawn carriages is unconstitutional, according to a federal lawsuit filed Thursday by a union that represents carriage owners and operators.
    • According to recent reports, the city council passed the ban Thursday, putting an end to a 168-year industry that has attracted a healthy tourist business.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that A recent New York City law banning horse-drawn carriages is unconstitutional, according to a federal lawsuit filed Thursday by a union that represents carriage owners and operators. (Photo from Shutterstock).

    A recent New York City law banning horse-drawn carriages is unconstitutional, according to a federal lawsuit filed Thursday by a union that represents carriage owners and operators.

    According to recent reports, the city council passed the ban Thursday, putting an end to a 168-year industry that has attracted a healthy tourist business. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani looks to sunset the carriages by June 1, 2028, in all five boroughs in the city. The union representing carriage operators and owners argues that their livelihood has been taken away and seeks to have the ban struck down.

    “The city’s approach can be summarized in 12 words: immediately cripple the owners, ignore property interests and contracts, and maybe compensate,” according to the suit.

    Sources indicate that additionally, the new law stipulates the “humane disposition” of the horses. Animal rights activists have in the past expressed concern over the welfare of the horses. Earlier this year, an 18-year-old tourist died after jumping from a runaway carriage—the first fatality since the carriages were introduced into Central Park in New York City.

    “Our city has changed, and now it is time for our laws to change, too,” Mamdani mentioned.

    Bloomberg Law and MSN had coverage.

    #227720. Nepal: Predatory Lending Abuses Exacerbated by Conflict in the Gulf

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2957 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hrw ↗ Open Full Page

    Nepal: Predatory Lending Abuses Exacerbated by Conflict in the Gulf

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2957 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that (Tokyo) – Authorities in Nepal should hold illegal moneylenders accountable for abuses against borrowers, including unlawful land dispossession, arbitrary eviction, threats and acts of violence, and sexual exploitation, Human Rights Watch said today.
    • “Despite government commitments to protect borrowers, illegal practices are rife in Nepal’s informal credit sector, leaving those with the fewest resources dependent on moneylenders who can take everything they own,” mentioned Meenakshi Ganguly, Asia deputy director at Human Rights Watch.
    • Human Rights Watch interviewed 18 borrowers, as well as local government officials, lawyers, and activists from six districts in the Terai region where informal money lending is rampant, reviewed government reports, and examined over 50 cases in Nawalparasi district.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that (Tokyo) – Authorities in Nepal should hold illegal moneylenders accountable for abuses against borrowers, including unlawful land dispossession, arbitrary eviction, threats and acts of violence, and sexual exploitation, Human Rights Watch said today. Conflicts in the Gulf region, where many Nepalis are migrant workers facing exorbitant recruitment fees, have made more people vulnerable to extortion by illegal lenders.

    “Despite government commitments to protect borrowers, illegal practices are rife in Nepal’s informal credit sector, leaving those with the fewest resources dependent on moneylenders who can take everything they own,” mentioned Meenakshi Ganguly, Asia deputy director at Human Rights Watch. “The government of Prime Minister Balendra Shah should carry out the government’s commitments to ensure that the law against fraudulent and abusive lending is consistently enforced.”.

    Human Rights Watch interviewed 18 borrowers, as well as local government officials, lawyers, and activists from six districts in the Terai region where informal money lending is rampant, reviewed government reports, and examined over 50 cases in Nawalparasi district.

    Human Rights Watch found that many families are struggling with unmanageable debt particularly as migrant workers in the Gulf States during 2026 have faced reduced incomes or involuntary travel delays ahead of starting jobs due to the conflict between the US, Israel, and Iran. War-induced disruption amplified pre-existing abuses, including reliance on unauthorized individual agents and unreasonable recruitment fees. Human Rights Watch previously found that companies in Gulf states play a critical role in driving these illegal costs by refusing to cover costs and fees to recruiters that they know will be borne by workers.

    Industry observers note that government investigations have shown that, under Nepal’s informal credit practices, a borrower signs or thumbprints an unsecured personal loan contract, known locally as kapali tamasuk, which can falsely list a principal amount three to ten times more than the cash received. These loans, known as meter byaj, in some cases compound at annual rates ranging from 36 percent to 60 percent or more, compared with less than 10 percent charged by banks.

    As low-income households that had relied on remittances disrupted by the war have shifted their limited resources toward expenses for food, fuel, and healthcare, they have been increasingly unable to repay their loans, leading to a surge in defaults. In response, some moneylenders are forcing evictions or land transfers, including through violence, in the worst cases tying people into generational debt. Nepal authorities are not pushing for effective long term solutions beyond encouraging and facilitating debtors and creditors to enter pre-court settlements.

    Following the outbreak of conflict in the Persian Gulf, in March 2026, the Nepal government suspended both institutional and individual labor permits to protect its citizens, including to Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, and Kuwait, with an estimated 2,000 Nepalis denied labor permits daily. Thousands were stopped from travelling at the international airport despite possessing valid medical clearances, verified visas, and binding employment contracts, while administrative delays also led foreign firms to cancel labor contracts. However, the authorities failed to step in to protect aspiring migrant laborers who still had to service their high interest meter byaj loans, leaving them exposed to violent enforcement by loan sharks.

    “They did not just hit my father to get the money,” mentioned one victim. “They beat him in the middle of the road during the day so that everyone else in the village would see what happens when you cannot pay the meter byaj. The local goons told us, ‘If you don’t sign over the land title today, your family will receive a corpse tomorrow.’”.

    It has been revealed that while abuses, including violent attacks and forced evictions, appear to be increasing due to conflict related disruptions, many moneylenders have long wielded political and economic power over borrowers. Claiming that the justice system routinely favors the moneylenders, borrowers have staged three extended protests in Kathmandu over the last four years—the longest for 442 days—and three long marches. Each time, the government agreed to resolve debt issues but failed to honor its commitments to protect victims. Consequently, the borrowers have regularly protested at district and provincial levels as well.

    Industry observers note that although government has criminalized such loans, borrowers and activists in Madhesh Province stated that police have repeatedly refused to file reports when victims seek protection. Instead, they said, the police typically dismiss abuses and intimidation by moneylenders as “private civil disputes.”.

    “When the moneylender came to break our door, we ran to the police, but the officers told us to go home and settle personal transactional disputes ourselves,” noted a Rautahat district migrant worker.

    The police also back moneylenders when they use signed blank checks and banking laws to threaten defaulters with arrest, or use informal deeds as the basis to seize land and evict families. “The lender made me sign a blank check when he gave me a loan, and later on he filled it for 10 lakhs (US$6,500) and sent the police to threaten me with jail when the check bounced,” said a Siraha district farmer.

    Borrowers also cite cases in which the authorities do not intervene even when lenders use patently unlawful loan agreements to obtain asset foreclosure orders. “The lender told me openly that he owns the courts and the administration,” remarked Shiv Shanker from Gaur, Rautahat district, who after facing abuses from a moneylender, is leading protests. “When the state shuts its doors on a poor farmer, death feels like the only place left to hide from this meter byaj.”.

    On May 5, 2023, the government criminalized informal loans as an “improper transaction,” and declared that forging loan contracts, threatening borrowers, or fabricating loan amounts, are punishable by up to seven years in prison. However, enforcement remains weak. Successive governments have established inquiry commissions to address the crisis, but over 65,000 complaints registered with inquiry commissions remain unresolved due to a lack of legal provisions and administrative bottlenecks.

    According to recent reports, these failures have contributed to deadly outcomes including suicide. Santidevi Mahato from Biratnagar died by suicide on June 21, following threats from a moneylender because she could not service her debt, people interviewed said. After borrowing 150,000 Nepali rupees (US$975) in October 2015, she had repaid 400,000 Nepali rupees (US$2,600) in installments. Yet, violating their agreement, the moneylender seized her land and threatened to evict her from her house.

    Under international human rights law and standards, governments have the obligation to take steps to protect people from serious rights abuses caused by private actors, such as moneylenders, including through investigating and prosecuting serious crimes.

    On July 17, the government led by Prime Minister Balendra Shah concluded a nine-point pact with protest leaders to eliminate predatory lending, after debt victims began a march to Kathmandu. The government should take immediate legal and policy steps to institutionalize its commitment, Human Rights Watch said. Nepal’s donors and international partners should assist the government to establish systematic debt relief, and grievance mechanisms that can support debt restructuring.

    “The Balendra Shah government was elected with the promise of change, to overturn existing oppressive structures,” Ganguly remarked. “More closely regulating moneylenders and ending their chokehold on farmers and laborers is a crucial step in ensuring lasting social justice.”.

    Nepal’s informal credit system is rooted in its feudal history, where local elites used predatory debt to trap peasants in tenancy and systems of generational servitude such as Kamaiya, Haliya, and Haruwa-Charuwa.

    It has been revealed that the present-day meter byaj system evolved around a spurt in labor migration during the decade-long civil war in Nepal, from 1996 to 2006, and rapidly spread after the 2007 political unrest in the Terai region. An estimated 7 million Nepalis work abroad, about half in India and a majority of the rest in Gulf countries, contributing a third of the national GDP. For many households, migration became one of the few viable ways to earn a living, while the absence of accessible and affordable institutional credit left them dependent on informal lenders to finance the costs of securing employment abroad.

    Industry observers note that some local moneylenders and corrupt agents demanded exorbitant fees to help rural youth find jobs abroad, particularly in the Gulf States and Malaysia. Land or property was borrowers’ main collateral, but they often later discovered that their contracts were fraudulent, including falsified sums and forged documents. The schemes exploited bureaucratic complicity at government land offices to transfer property titles despite contracts being illegal, and borrowers lost their assets due to a lack of protection from the government.

    It has been revealed that in interviews, debt victims described devastating cycles in which migrant workers are forever bound to serving a predatory moneylender, while the authorities fail to intervene. Ramnath Musahar from Susta, Nawalparasi district, said the family borrowed to send two of his brothers to work in the Gulf States in 2015, but despite servicing the loan, their debt had grown enormously:.

    In a recent development, my brothers sent back Rs. 1,200,000 (US$8,000) from their wages, and we sold our plots [of land] to pay an extra Rs. 1,800,000 (US$11,000). But the lender went to the district court with a fake contract and claimed we still owe him Rs. 5,000,000 (US$33,000). The court looked only at the paper and our thumbprints; it did not look at our tears. The police came and threw our belongings into the dirt. We went from being independent farmers to beggars overnight.

    Since the US and Israel began their assault on Iran on February 28, 2026, and Iran subsequently blocked and attacked ships traveling through the Strait of Hormuz and attacked sites across the Gulf States, the fallout is being felt far beyond the region.

    In a recent development, in Nepal, UN agencies warned that “rising fuel prices, closure of shipping routes, and growing financial uncertainty are placing mounting pressure on economies, labor markets and vulnerable households.” According to the World Bank, Nepal’s real GDP growth could fall from 3.67 percent in 2024 to 2.3 percent in 2026 due to reduced tourism, higher transport costs, and supply chain snags. Rising inflation, a weakening currency leading to a rise in import costs, a spike in fuel costs, and stalled fertilizer supply have placed additional pressure on low-income households, and increased demands for overseas employment.

    Hoping to seek jobs to support their families, many rural youths have taken loans from loan sharks, who have responded by raising rates. Many families were stuck servicing those loans, even as people were unable to travel because of conflict-related disruptions.

    It has been revealed that workers already employed in the Gulf States are facing job losses, unpaid leave, wage reductions, and other disruptions that have reduced their ability to keep sending remittances. Compared with the same period the previous year, Gulf-bound labor approvals plummeted by 52 percent—from 228,165 down to 109,249—between the outbreak of the war in late February and mid-September, according to Department of Foreign Employment data. At least two Nepali workers have been killed due to the conflict, and 15 injured.

    Many are returning to Nepal stripped of their anticipated income, and unable to service their loans. The authorities have failed to act as moneylenders crack down on defaulters, beating them, evicting them, and forcing land or asset transfers. The lenders are also seeking court-ordered asset foreclosures and even arrest warrants based on the loan contracts, including contracts that borrowers alleged contained fabricated loan amounts. As a Mahotari district borrower observed, “The law notes meter byaj is a crime, but police demanded receipts I never got, so the thief walks free, and I am made the criminal.”.

    Women-led households, Dalits (considered an “untouchable” caste), and Indigenous ethnic communities have even fewer protections from violence such as beatings and sexual violence due to their caste, gender, and discrimination. One woman from Dhanusha district remarked she was raped by a moneylender under threat of eviction.

    My husband was trapped in a labor camp abroad and couldn’t send money. The lender came to my house with the contract and mentioned he would evict my children the next morning unless I “compromised” with him. He held our roof over my head like a weapon. I had to endure his abuse in silence because a poor woman in this village has no voice against a powerful man who holds her land paper.

    While the conflict has exacerbated the crisis, debt-ridden families had already proliferated in Nepal, particularly in Terai districts. The authorities have failed to protect these families.

    Chirai Chamar, a widowed Dalit worker in Paklihawa, Nawalparasi district, while struggling to gain control of her inherited family land, had borrowed 20,000 Nepali rupees (US$130). A moneylender offered to help with the legalities in exchange for a portion of that land. “A moneylender, from whom I had borrowed Rs. 20,000, came to me saying he will help me to acquire all the papers required to own my family land, and in return I need to give him two katthas (650 square meters) of land,” she stated.

    Recent findings suggest that he then grabbed an additional four katthas (1336 square meters), paying Chamar a grossly undervalued sum of Rs. 150,000 (US$970). When rights activists intervened to reclaim Chamar’s land and restore her livelihood, local thugs threatened them and destroyed Chamar’s crops. Despite complaints, the police and the local officials failed to assist her.

    Ashamaya (name changed), a resident of Thecho, Lalitpur, supported her family by running a small tea shop. However, when her father-in-law fell ill, she had to close the business to care for him. Left without income as the medical expenses mounted, she borrowed money from a moneylender, who charged an extortionate annual interest rate of 120 percent, which she could not pay. Under pressure, she took on another usurious loan simply to pay off the old one.

    Although she settled that debt by selling a piece of land, she had to borrow again, this time to cover her husband’s medical costs, but she no longer had enough land for collateral. The moneylender coerced her into sex with multiple men after he forced her to sign a new contact for Rs. 2500,000 (UDS$16,167), amounting to five times her initial debt.

    It has been revealed that debt victims have started to organize under various banners and groups, demanding that the government protect them from abusive loan sharks. In 2022, after hundreds walked barefoot for weeks from districts including Siraha, Dhanusha, Mahottari, Sarlahi, Kapilvastu, and Nawalparasi to stage protests in Kathmandu, the government at that time establisheda three-member Commission for the Investigation of Loan Sharking (CILS) in April 2023, to collect complaints, study structural issues, and resolve loan-sharking disputes.

    Recent findings suggest that by May 21, 2023, when the District Administration Offices stopped accepting these complaints, over 28,000 had been filed across 67 districts, with an alarming 21,552 cases concentrated in Madhesh Province. However, the commission only resolved and closed 5,115 loan disputes. Several victims reported abuses by district offices. “We went to the Chief District Officer expecting justice, but instead, the police and the lender ganged up on us, warned us that going to court would mean total land auction, and scared us into signing an agreement to pay half the inflated sum,” stated a woman from Siraha.

    Sources indicate that as complaints persisted, including of violent encounters in which the police failed to intervene, the authorities largely resorted to symbolic agreements with the victims, followed by the repeated formation of fresh commissions. A commission was set up in March 2024, led by former high court judge Tej Bahadur Karki, and another in March 2025, led by Baburam Regmi. In November 2025, the Regmi Commission reported a total of 41,409 complaints registered in 43 districts. Of these, 6,393 cases had been resolved, while 35,016 complaints remain pending.

    Each commission exposed the vast scale of the crisis but political commitments to break the stranglehold of moneylenders remain unfulfilled. Nawalparasi’s Deputy Chief District Officer Poshan Raj Bhandari told Human Rights Watch that, “The existing law will not be enough to resolve this problem; the government needs to think of a separate legal process to resolve this.”.

    According to recent reports, when Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s government was elected in March 2026 with a large majority, victims had cause for hope. However, instead of the government ensuring a collective debt moratorium, victims say that moneylenders have convinced the police to matter a surge of arrest warrants against debtors.

    In response, victims have organized new protests. Nigra Nabin, a leader of the protest movement, mentioned that based on “past experiences” the victims “had three long-standing demands” including the nullification of all illegal agreements and the underlying loan contracts that support them; a new law to institutionalize these actions and establish special legal procedures; and a separate entity dedicated to ensuring justice for the victims.

    On July 9, the anti-loan shark movement began an 11-day justice march from Janakpur to Kathmandu. On the sixth day of the march, Home Affairs Minister Sudhan Gurung traveled to Nijgadh to hold direct talks with the protesters. Following three days of negotiations, the government accepted the three core demands and signed an updated nine-point deal, leading the protesters to call off the march.

    It has been revealed that the victims are waiting. One of them, Sobita Devi Mahato, said: “If this is not resolved, the only resort I have is to go to the Home Ministry and hang myself there.”.

    Modi’s Authoritarian Playbook in India.

    Germany: Funding Cuts Threaten Anti-Discrimination Efforts

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (900 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (Berlin, November 26, 2026) – The German government’s decision to discontinue funding for dozens of civil society projects, following budget cuts, undermines Germany’s efforts to address racism, discrimination, and antisemitism and protect human rights, Human Rights Watch mentioned today.
    • In a recent development, “The German government’s cuts undermine critical civil society work and networks that directly protect human rights and combat the threats from the far-right,” said Almaz Teffera, senior Europe researcher at Human Rights Watch.
    • Sources indicate that on November 12, the Bundestag’s budgetary committee approved the government’s proposed cuts of about €20 million to the federal civil society democracy fund, “Live Democracy!” (“Demokratie Leben!”).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (Berlin, November 26, 2026) – The German government’s decision to discontinue funding for dozens of civil society projects, following budget cuts, undermines Germany’s efforts to address racism, discrimination, and antisemitism and protect human rights, Human Rights Watch mentioned today. The German government and Bundestag should release further funds to guarantee the continuation of dozens of essential civil society projects. The Bundestag is due to vote on the federal budget on November 27, 2026.

    In a recent development, “The German government’s cuts undermine critical civil society work and networks that directly protect human rights and combat the threats from the far-right,” said Almaz Teffera, senior Europe researcher at Human Rights Watch. “The German government and Bundestag should remedy the cuts in the federal budget by providing funds to save trusted anti-discrimination and anti-extremism work that directly protects and empowers people at this critical time.”.

    Sources indicate that on November 12, the Bundestag’s budgetary committee approved the government’s proposed cuts of about €20 million to the federal civil society democracy fund, “Live Democracy!” (“Demokratie Leben!”). On November 13, the government sent funding rejections to dozens of trusted civil society projects that monitor and document discrimination and hate crimes, foster civic engagement and education, and support victims and those at risk amid alarming levels of hate crimes.

    Sources indicate that in March, the government announced that it intended to restructure the Live Democracy! program and required all funded initiatives and projects to reapply. The government introduced fresh criteria and objectives, which the education and family affairs minister, Karin Prien, noted would mean funded initiatives “reach the silent majority [in society], which is in danger of turning away from democracy.” The cuts undermine the work of civil society groups that advocate for human rights, diversity, and democracy.

    Live Democracy! began in 2015 as a response to racially motivated right-wing extremist terror cases in Germany in the early 2000s and subsequent institutional failures. The program had supported civil society groups, initiatives, and structures to push back against extremism, racism, and antisemitism, aiming to strengthen Germany’s democracy, promote diversity, and prevent extremism. Prien removed the goal of promoting diversity, claiming that it was “not a sufficient funding objective” on its own. Projects on racism, antisemitism, or other hostility against a group fall under the category of preventing extremism, with a restricted list of potentially fundable activities.

    Recent findings suggest that according to media reports, the government invited only 150 out of 1,200 applicants who expressed interest in funding to submit a full funding application. The program had previously funded about 600 projects. Several applications for projects on anti-Black and anti-Muslim racism as well as antisemitism and right-wing extremism received partial or full rejections.

    Previous funding from Live Democracy! was used by civil society groups like CLAIM, which works to combat anti-Muslim racism and hatred, to partially finance vital civil society monitoring and documentation infrastructure to track anti-Muslim discrimination and hate incidents. The group stated that discontinuing their funding puts Muslim people in Germany at risk at a time when anti-Muslim incidents are at a record high.

    Project funding for Each One Teach One, a group that empowers Black people in Germany and conducts surveys of anti-Black racism, was also rejected. Funding was cut 60 percent for other projects countering right-wing extremism. Groups mentioned the funding cuts demonstrated a lack of political will to defend democracy.

    Industry observers note that in January, Prien had spoken about education as a key driver to counter antisemitism, yet educational projects on antisemitism that had been funded also received negative decisions. Unexpectedly, on November 20, three projects on antisemitism that had initially received rejections were told they would be funded.

    While civil society groups have no guarantee of public funding, governments should create clear, transparent, and nondiscriminatory funding criteria and processes that prevent arbitrary funding decisions, Human Rights Watch said. Governments should not use funding decisions to sanction groups for their legitimate advocacy and criticism of government policies.

    In February 2025, the conservative bloc of Christian Democratic Union/Christian Social Union, of which Prien is a member, had sought to delegitimize more than a dozen nongovernmental organizations after they criticized the bloc’s willingness to pass a parliamentary motion on migration with votes of the far-right political party, Alternative for Germany. The bloc alleged that these groups violated so-called “political neutrality,” falsely suggesting that groups that receive public funds should not engage in political debates or advocacy.

    Civil society groups are essential for monitoring human rights and holding states to account to meet their obligations under international and regional human rights law, including the elimination of racial discrimination. In line with the right to freedom of association, groups have a right of access to funding on a fair and nondiscriminatory basis, Human Rights Watch said.

    “Cutting funds for essential civil society work when it is needed most sends the wrong message,” Teffera stated. “Germany’s federal government and Bundestag should recognize that funding civil society work is an essential investment in the defense of human rights, rule of law, and democracy.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • (The Hague) – Member countries of the International Criminal Court (ICC) should prioritize measures to promote and protect the court and those cooperating with it, Human Rights Watch said in a report released today.
    • It has been revealed that this year’s session takes place as the court and the broader international justice system face unrelenting pressure from the United States.
    • According to recent reports, “The start of the Duterte trial at the same time as the annual ICC Assembly session should remind member countries of the court’s critical importance,” said Liz Evenson, international justice director at Human Rights Watch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    (The Hague) – Member countries of the International Criminal Court (ICC) should prioritize measures to promote and protect the court and those cooperating with it, Human Rights Watch said in a report released today. The 24-page report makes detailed recommendations for the annual session of the ICC’s Assembly of States Parties, which will convene in The Hague from November 30 to December 7, 2026.

    It has been revealed that this year’s session takes place as the court and the broader international justice system face unrelenting pressure from the United States. On October 9, the US government escalated its campaign to destroy the ICC “brick by brick” by imposing sanctions on the whole court under a February 2025 executive order. This followed the sanctioning of ICC judges and prosecutors, a United Nations human rights expert, and three leading Palestinian rights organizations. Yet, the ICC continues to advance its critical work for justice. The landmark trial of former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte is scheduled to begin on November 30.

    According to recent reports, “The start of the Duterte trial at the same time as the annual ICC Assembly session should remind member countries of the court’s critical importance,” said Liz Evenson, international justice director at Human Rights Watch. “At the session, member countries should stand firmly by the court and not take steps that could curtail victims’ access to justice.”.

    In his October 9 announcement, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated the sanctions were aimed at shielding US nationals from investigation and prosecution at the ICC. The Trump administration has previously objected to the court’s investigation of Israeli nationals for their conduct in Palestine. The ICC has issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for serious crimes in Gaza.

    Industry observers note that after a China-Russia-US summit––at which the three countries’ leaders adopted a declaration that included expressing concern for state consent and the immunity of state officials, and that the ICC and other similar bodies should not “abuse their jurisdiction”––US President Donald Trump on November 20 remarked that Russian President Vladimir Putin “especially is not happy with” the ICC. Putin faces war crimes charges before the ICC for the unlawful deportation and forcible transfer of children from occupied areas of Ukraine to Russia.

    Industry observers note that the US government has pitched the court-wide sanctions as “structured ... to provide an opportunity for States Parties to negotiate and present a solution to address” its “concerns.” The authorization of certain transactions with the court for a six-month period, which otherwise would have been immediately affected by the court-wide sanctions, is an ultimatum to member countries to meet the US government’s demands; but these demands effectively allow the Trump administration to determine whom the court can prosecute, Human Rights Watch remarked.

    Industry observers note that in the lead-up to the Assembly session, media reports referred to concerning proposals by some countries to meet US demands, including curbing the court’s jurisdiction over nationals of nonmember countries or exempting heads of state from the court’s reach. Offering the US government solutions that would hollow out the court’s mandate and guarantee impunity for certain powerful individuals would severely undermine the legitimacy and credibility of the ICC and the international justice system, Human Rights Watch said.

    According to recent reports, at the Assembly session, ICC member countries should focus on safeguarding the court’s independence and taking concrete actions to protect the ICC and those cooperating with it. This should include calling on the European Union to urgently activate its Blocking Statute, which aims to shield European operators from the effects of extraterritorial sanctions, Human Rights Watch remarked.

    Recent findings suggest that seven lawsuits have been brought in US federal court over the US sanctions targeting the ICC and those supporting its work. Human Rights Watch, together with three other human rights organizations, filed one of these lawsuits on August 11, seeking to have the sanctions regime struck down. A wide range of human rights organizations, other experts, and former US government officials have filed amicus (friend of the court) briefs in support of the suit.

    The United States is also stepping up diplomatic pressure on ICC member countries to leave the court. Over the past year, seven countries—Niger, Burkina Faso, Mali, Venezuela, Chad, Naoero and Tajikistan—decided to withdraw from the ICC. While not all of these withdrawals can be linked to US pressure, they undermine efforts to achieve the global adoption of the court’s founding treaty, the Rome Statute. Tajikistan’s notification of withdrawal on November 20 followed its failure, for a second time, to arrest Putin when he was visiting the country and surrender him to the court, as required by its obligations as an ICC member. The Tajik parliament had adopted legislation on withdrawal in October.

    “US efforts to press countries to withdraw from the Rome Statute are both an attack on states that have chosen to become ICC members and on international justice itself,” Evenson said. “The Trump administration has little standing with respect to either.”.

    At the upcoming session, ICC members should call on the countries that have withdrawn to reconsider their decisions and remain part of the court. They should also engage with other ICC members to develop strategies to counter US pressure and promote a unified community of member countries, Human Rights Watch stated.

    Other issues on the Assembly’s agenda include electing 6 of the court’s 18 judges and making decisions on the process for the election of the court’s next prosecutor, expected to be held in December 2027. On July 24, 2026, the Assembly removed ICC Prosecutor Karim Khan from office for serious misconduct and serious breach of duty. Member countries should focus on merit and the most qualified candidates as they make decisions about elections that will shape the future of the court, Human Rights Watch said.

    “The ICC’s daily work as grave abuses continue around the world is proof of the urgent need to protect the global rule of law,” Evenson said. “Member countries should demonstrate that they reject the idea of a world where might makes right and use their annual meeting to stand for ensuring no one is above the law.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On August 4, 2006, 17 Sri Lankan staff members of the Paris-based humanitarian organization Action Contre la Faim (Action Against Hunger) were summarily executed at their office in Muttur, Sri Lanka. Over 20 years later, this unresolved case is emblematic of attacks on humanitarian workers during the country’s brutal civil war that ended in 2009.

    A new report by the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, “I Died Many Times”; Attacks on Humanitarian Assistance in Sri Lanka, documents the numerous threats aid workers faced during the final years of Sri Lanka’s civil war with the separatist Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam.

    According to recent reports, the report finds that the government purposefully shut down humanitarian space “as a slow, deliberate strangulation” that effectively cordoned civilians into government-held areas, preventing independent observers from witnessing war crimes by the warring parties. The report, which is the latest from the UN’s Sri Lanka Accountability Project to gather evidence of international crimes in Sri Lanka, also finds “that impunity has resulted not from isolated failures, but from mutually reinforcing practices that have repeatedly frustrated accountability.”.

    Industry observers note that the UN identifies four causes of impunity. First, it notes the state’s denial of responsibility. Second, the persistent failure of domestic investigations and prosecutions to deliver accountability. Third, it documents threats to victims, witnesses, and experts and the lack of effective witness protection in Sri Lanka. Lastly, it notes the appointment of presidential commissions of inquiry by successive governments instead of pursuing effective prosecutions.

    Sri Lanka’s 26-year civil war was marked by serious human rights abuses and war crimes by both sides. Despite numerous domestic, international, and UN investigations, there has been no justice.

    While President Anura Kumara Dissanayake took office in September 2024 promising justice for past rights abuses, most victims remain without answers or accountability because of the government’s failure to bring legal and structural reforms, including the promised independent public prosecutor’s office. The government has also refused to accept the Sri Lanka Accountability Project, which was established by the UN Human Rights Council in 2021 to collect evidence of serious rights abuses for use in possible future trials. This report shows why the UN’s evidence collection in Sri Lanka is as key as ever.

    A Florida judge has sentenced a prominent plastic surgeon to death for the murder of a “beloved” lawyer who went missing in 2023, saying the doctor committed the crime in a “cold, calculated and premeditated manner.”.

    Pinellas County Circuit Judge Joseph A. Bulone handed down the death sentence Friday to Dr. Tomasz Kosowski of Florida, who was convicted in September of murdering attorney Steven Cozzi, 41, whom he faced in a contentious lawsuit, Law360 reports.

    Prosecutors said Cozzi was last seen entering the restroom of his law office in Largo, Florida, in March 2023. Surveillance video allegedly captured Kosowski walking into the law office’s main entrance on the morning that Cozzi went missing, showing the surgeon carrying a backpack and a large box. About two hours later, the video shows him walking out of the building with a different clothes and pulling a large cart covered with a red blanket.

    Recent findings suggest that cozzi, described as a “beloved” person, worked for Blanchard Law, a small law firm specializing in business litigation, bankruptcies and contract disputes. At the time of his disappearance, Cozzi was representing a defendant being sued by Kosowski over medical billing disputes. His body was never found.

    Free Education Is Key to Ending Child Marriage

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (496 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Hrw

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, on November 27, the world marks the first International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage – a chance to end a practice that robs children of their childhood and prospects.
    • Free education is a powerful tool to help prevent it.
    • According to recent reports, and prevention needs to start earlier.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, on November 27, the world marks the first International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage – a chance to end a practice that robs children of their childhood and prospects. Every year, 12 million girls are married before 18 – that’s one every three seconds.

    Free education is a powerful tool to help prevent it. UNICEF estimates that if all girls completed secondary education, it could cut child marriage by two-thirds. Yet school fees and indirect costs — uniforms, transport, books, examinations — force girls out of school and into early marriage. Free secondary education helps keep girls in school through adolescence, when the risk of child marriage is greatest. Evidence from 14 African countries indicates that making lower secondary education free and compulsory raised girls’ educational attainment by 1.6 years.

    According to recent reports, and prevention needs to start earlier. A study published this month, covering women across 117 countries, found that legal guarantees of pre-primary education were associated with higher rates of school completion among girls and lower rates of child marriage and adolescent childbearing. Yet UNESCO reports that only 68 percent of countries and 46 percent of low-income countries legally guarantee tuition-free pre-primary education.

    Free education from pre-primary through secondary forms a continuous pathway to opportunity and empowerment.

    Sources indicate that sierra Leone indicates what political leadership can achieve on both fronts. Its First Lady spearheaded this International Day, while its education ministers and diplomats have championed a latest treaty on free education at the United Nations. Domestically, it has guaranteed 13 years of free education, from pre-primary through secondary, since 2023 and banned child marriage in 2024.

    In a recent development, international law needs to catch up. The Convention on the Rights of the Child neither explicitly recognizes a right to early childhood care and education nor guarantees free pre-primary and secondary education for all. Sierra Leone, the Dominican Republic, Bulgaria and ten other countries are therefore advancing a fresh Optional Protocol to close these gaps. A binding commitment would strengthen accountability and drive national reforms. Negotiations on this proposed treaty will continue in October 2027.

    On this inaugural International Day, Sierra Leone, supported by 14 countries, will bring diplomats, experts, and child advocates together in Geneva. Investing in free education advances girls’ rights, dignity, and futures – and is a decisive step towards ending child marriage. By supporting the Optional Protocol at the United Nations, states will be making a clear statement that they stand against child marriage and are committed to delivering a freer and fairer world for girls.

    Congress last enacted a significant expansion of the federal courts in 1990, according to a story by Law360.

    Sources indicate that the federal courts presently have 677 district judgeships and 179 appellate judgeships. Under the bill, judgeships would be added in a number of states, including Arizona, California, Iowa, New Jersey and New York.

    In a recent development, the U.S. House of Representatives and the U.S. Senate passed a version of the bill in 2024, but then-President Joe Biden vetoed it during his last few weeks in office.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Featured image credit:  Jack English/Apple TV+ via Rolling Stone.
    • Slow Horses, the wonderful television series based on Mick Herron’s wonderful Slough House books series has been renewed.
    • Sources indicate that but the series has been renewed even further than that.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Featured image credit:  Jack English/Apple TV+ via Rolling Stone.

    Industry observers note that yes. Slow Horses, the wonderful television series based on Mick Herron’s wonderful Slough House books series has been renewed. Season 6 just aired this fall, on its home network of Apple TV+, and work on the 7th season has begun.

    Sources indicate that but the series has been renewed even further than that. When Season 6 aired, we learned that the show had been renewed for an 8th season. This was great news.

    Recent findings suggest that and now, Apple has announced that the series will continue through Season 10! Yes, Seasons 9 and 10 have been announced! This means we have four more seasons to look forward to. That’s four more years of Jackson Lamb and his crew of misfits. That’s a whole American presidential term’s worth of Slow Horses.

    In a recent development, until Season 6, each season of the show has adapted a single one of Heron’s novels, all in chronological order. Season 6 broke the mold by adapting two: the sequential volumes Joe Country and Slough House. This means there are two extant novels left to adapt, Bad Actors and Clown Town, and early reports have confirmed that seasons 7 and 8 will undertake each of those novels, respectively. This means that Heron’s next novel will also be guaranteed a season, as will the next.

    Industry observers note that will he indeed write more? Yes, it certainly seems so, though there have been no announcements about a new installment. The most recent novel, Clown Town, was released in 2025, and Heron’s novels typically have a 1-3 year gap in between them. But there’s still plenty of relevant Slough House material rife for adaptation; Heron has also published five Slough House novellas, none of which have been adapted yet. (Interested readers should note that all the novellas thus far have been collected in a volume called Standing By the Wall.).

    It has been revealed that the series Slow Horses stars Gary Oldman as the irascible, perpetually-disheveled, foul-mouthed, flatulent and yet thoroughly lovable MI5 agent Jackson Lamb, who oversees a notorious departmental backwater of the Secret Service called Slough House, an institutional repository for agents who have badly messed up (or pissed off somebody important). Time and time again Lamb and his team of oddballs, including Jack Lowden’s put-in-Slough-House-by-sabotage River Cartwright, wind up using their special skills, disregard for the rules, and occasional desire to prove themselves/not be messed with to save the day, often. It’s the best.

She has a PhD from the departments of English/comparative literature and theatre at Columbia University, where she was the Marion E. Ponsford fellow. She hosts the podcasst "Culture Schlock" at Lit Hub Radio. She is on instagram at @oldebean, twitter at @oldrutigliano, and bluesky at @oliviarutigliano.bsky.social.
