    Justice Department Introduces Largest-Ever Crackdown on Scammers, Targeting Over 800 Defendants to Protect Americans from Fraud

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2746 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fbi

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Today, the Justice Department declared the results of a historic surge in resources to protect Americans from criminal scam networks and online fraud following President Trump’s Executive Order 14390 directing a government-wide crackdown.
    • These actions include upcoming charges, extraditions, guilty verdicts, and criminal sentences.
    • According to recent reports, “Predatory scams against the American people will not be tolerated,” mentioned Attorney General Todd Blanche.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Today, the Justice Department declared the results of a historic surge in resources to protect Americans from criminal scam networks and online fraud following President Trump’s Executive Order 14390 directing a government-wide crackdown. Since the Executive Order was signed on March 6, Justice Department prosecutors have taken action to protect Americans in over 400 cases against over 800 defendants.

    These actions include upcoming charges, extraditions, guilty verdicts, and criminal sentences. U.S. prosecutors and agents also assisted law enforcement in over 10 countries in raids of foreign scam call centers and compounds that targeted Americans.

    According to recent reports, “Predatory scams against the American people will not be tolerated,” mentioned Attorney General Todd Blanche. “The unprecedented results of this surge are just the beginning. We will continue prosecuting those who perpetrate these schemes and disrupting the activities of transnational criminal organizations before they reach American shores.”.

    According to recent reports, “Under President Trump’s Executive Order 14390, this FBI has made dismantling predatory scam enterprises a top priority using a whole-of-government approach,” remarked FBI Director Kash Patel. “Through Operation Blackout, this FBI’s scam center demolition initiative, we’ve seized nearly $17 billion in illicit funds, taken more than 14,000 digital devices, directly warned over 11,000 Americans from scam attempts, and prevented more than $690 million in potential victim losses. The Trump Administration is crushing scam centers plaguing Americans, and with Attorney General Blanche and our interagency partners, we are delivering on this righteous mission every day all over the world. The message to these scam syndicates is clear: if you target Americans, justice will find you.”.

    It has been revealed that “Scammers worldwide steal billions of dollars from Americans each year, profiting from lies and vulnerability,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “Under President Trump and Attorney General Blanche, the Criminal Division is taking the fight directly to the criminal networks that are stealing from Americans. We will not allow these scammers to hide behind their screens or escape justice by committing these crimes abroad. The Justice Department will use every tool at its disposal to disrupt predatory schemes, punish wrongdoers, and protect the American people.”.

    In a recent development, according to Gallup, 10% of U.S. adults experienced a scam last year, either directly or through someone in their household. Nearly three in four scam victims experienced a negative effect on their mental health or well-being. Gallup also reports that Americans lost an estimated $68 billion to scams in 2025 alone. These scams include cryptocurrency investment scams, financially motivated sextortion, government imposter schemes, and other predatory schemes that collectively cost Americans billions of dollars, with many families losing their life savings.

    In one scam charged this month, current and former members of prison gangs in Georgia used contraband mobile phones to falsely tell victims that they missed jury duty and would be arrested if they failed to pay a “fine.” 14 individuals were charged in three indictments in federal and state courts for participation in these schemes, and another 17 defendants were charged in state court for a scheme to smuggle contraband mobile phones, often used to perpetrate fraud schemes and other crimes, into Georgia prisons. Websites that were used by inmates to commit jury duty imposter schemes were seized. Below are social media posts by Georgia prison inmates flaunting the proceeds of fraud schemes and contraband mobile phones used to contact victims.

    The anti-scam surge was coordinated by the Justice Department's Criminal Division, which brought together a dedicated team of prosecutors to identify scammers, disrupt their networks, and hold them accountable. This team includes experts across the Criminal Division’s sections, including the White Collar and Corporate Enforcement Section, Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section, Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section, Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Human Rights and Special Prosecutions Section, Office of Overseas Prosecutorial Development, Assistance and Training, and the Office of International Affairs.

    In a recent development, the whole-of-government approach includes initiatives by the FBI, State Department, Department of Homeland Security, including Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) and U.S. Secret Service, Treasury Department, U.S. Postal Inspection Service (USPIS), Federal Communications Commission, Federal Trade Commission (FTC), Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, and Internal Revenue Service (IRS).

    Sources indicate that during the surge period from March 6 to present, Assistant U.S. Attorneys and Criminal Division trial attorneys contributed to the surge by obtaining wide-ranging results in 85 federal districts across the country. 30 defendants were extradited to face scam-related charges in U.S. courts. Information about each case is highlighted on this interactive map.

    In the month leading up to today’s announcement alone, the Criminal Division filed and unsealed charges against over 30 scam defendants. In addition to the jury duty scam described above, additional schemes alleged and charged in these cases include:.

    More details on each scheme and additional Criminal Division surge actions are provided here.

    The Justice Department coordinated with other agencies to launch a public education and messaging campaign informing consumers of the dangers of fraud, providing guidance on avoiding schemes, and encouraging Americans to use the upcoming holiday season to “Share Your Scam Story” with friends and relatives.

    Industry observers note that operation Blackout is the FBI’s global counter-scam demolition initiative. Through intelligence-driven operations and close collaboration with international law enforcement and government partners, the FBI has restrained nearly $17 billion in illicit funds, seized more than 14,000 digital devices, and helped identify, disrupt, and dismantle over 29 scam compounds operating across Asia, Africa, and the Middle East. These operations resulted in the federal charging of more than 50 scam actors, while FBI coordination and investigative support enabled foreign partners to arrest or detain more than 320 additional perpetrators overseas.

    Sources indicate that working alongside international partners, the FBI also assisted in the liberation and repatriation of more than 2,200 trafficked workers forced to operate inside scam compounds. Since Executive Order 14390 on March 6th, Operation Level Up has prevented more than $143 million in victim losses, warned thousands of Americans they were being targeted by a scammer and frozen over $350 million in assets through FBI’s Recovery Asset Team.

    It has been revealed that as part of this coordinated global effort, the State Department funds U.S. law enforcement advisors who train and mentor foreign investigators and prosecutors to work on U.S. cases. In Southeast Asia, advisors mentor and provide technical assistance to local law enforcement on scam investigations. To date, the State Department funded and supported U.S. and Southeast Asian law enforcement to facilitate the freezing of more than $1 billion in stolen cryptocurrency, the takedown of over 1.4 million fraudulent websites and accounts, numerous arrests, and several pending extraditions. State Department-funded forensic tools helped analyze more than 10,000 devices and hard drives in Thailand alone, allowing U.S. and Thai law enforcement to better understand the criminal networks and advance U.S. investigations.

    In Moldova, the State Department trained local prosecutors who oversaw the October arrests of three suspects in an online romance scheme that took $440,000 from American and European victims in a single month. Additionally, the State Department provided investigative training, protective equipment, and forensics software that enabled raids in October that resulted in the closure of five call centers and detained eight suspected coordinators who allegedly ran fake cryptocurrency trading platforms that defrauded investors.

    Recent findings suggest that "Too many Americans have suffered from cyber fraud, particularly from scam operations emanating from Southeast Asia, and expanding across South Asia, the Middle East, Africa, and the Pacific. But the true cost is not in dollars alone. Behind every statistic is a human story – a family bankrupted, a retiree left destitute, or a young person driven to suicide," noted Deputy Assistant Secretary of State David Bedard. "We know the threat is evolving, and we are prepared to develop new tools and strategies to prevent scammers and other criminals from stealing from and harming Americans. Cyber-enabled fraud is proliferating around the world, so we must stay vigilant and build partnerships to combat it.".

    Homeland Security Investigations.

    According to recent reports, since March 6, HSI offices nationwide executed more than 300 arrests, worked with the Justice Department to indict more than 100 defendants, and secured approximately 80 convictions and guilty pleas. HSI’s financial fraud investigations have also resulted in the seizure, restraint, freezing, or recovery of more than $120 million dollars in illicit proceeds, including funds held in bank and cryptocurrency accounts, cash, precious metals, vehicles, real property, and other assets. HSI works with domestic and international law enforcement partners, prosecutors, financial institutions, and private-sector stakeholders to identify and dismantle the criminal networks responsible, trace and recover illicit proceeds, and pursue the return of funds to victims when legally authorized.

    “HSI is committed to identifying and dismantling the criminal networks that perpetrate these crimes, wherever they operate, while tracing and seizing illicit proceeds and pursuing the return of funds to victims whenever legally authorized,” said HSI Acting Executive Associate Director John A. Condon. “Through close coordination with our domestic and international law enforcement partners, prosecutors, financial institutions, and private-sector stakeholders, HSI will continue to hold these actors accountable and protect the American public from evolving financial threats.”.

    During the surge period, Secret Service investigators have restrained more than $200 million in illicit funds, disrupted 1,780 domains operated by scammers, and recovered more than $119 million while investigating more than 1,540 business email compromise incidents. Secret Service-led cases included the identification of a cryptocurrency investment conspiracy operated from scam centers in Cambodia that targeted at least 174 U.S. victims. In October, a Chinese national was extradited from the Netherlands and arraigned in the Central District of California for his alleged role in that conspiracy.

    “While we are encouraged by the progress made to date, our investigators continue to lead dozens of cases involving transnational criminal networks targeting the American people,” said U.S. Secret Service Director Sean Curran. “Today’s announcement demonstrates that scammers operating anywhere in the world can be identified and brought to justice. The Secret Service remains committed to its founding mission of investigating financial crimes and will continue to work with law enforcement partners in the United States and around the world to dismantle and disrupt these criminal networks.”.

    During the surge period, USPIS supported cases against dozens of defendants, including those who perpetrated jury duty imposter schemes described above, lottery and sweepstakes fraud, inheritance fraud, and fraud against Spanish-speaking Americans. Several of these cases involved prosecutions of list brokers who knowingly provided the names of elderly Americans to fraudsters operating abroad. USPIS also seized three internet domains linked to jury duty imposter schemes perpetrated by Georgia prison inmates. Traffic to all three web addresses was redirected to official government servers displaying a public seizure banner. This coordinated takedown effectively dismantled the operators’ digital infrastructure and prevented further public victimization. USPIS also partnered with the Justice Department to mail out over 4,800 unlicensed money transmitter letters since March, which has had an incredible impact on the rates of reducing recidivism for “money mules.”.

    “Behind every scam is a person whose financial security, trust, and peace of mind have been threatened,” noted Chief Inspector Gary Barksdale. “The Postal Inspection Service brings investigative expertise, nationwide reach, and a longstanding commitment to protecting consumers to this effort. Together with the Department of Justice and our partners, the USPIS is working to disrupt these criminal networks, pursue accountability, and prevent others from becoming victims.”.

    During the surge period, the FTC filed 16 actions challenging deceptive earnings claims, unfair payment processing practices, tech support scams, debt relief schemes, unauthorized billing practices, misleading claims about health products, health insurance frauds, government and business impersonations, and deceptive claims about sextortion assistance services. The FTC sent warning letters to a dozen websites advising them of their obligations to comply with the TAKE IT DOWN Act and to 25 companies that market or generate sales leads for healthcare plans, putting them on notice about deceptive or unfair claims that likely violate laws enforced by the FTC. The FTC has continued to work with domain registrars and others to take down social media pages and 19 websites impersonating the FTC or FTC officials. Since April 2026, the FTC has connected more than 365 callers to the Justice Department’s National Elder Fraud Hotline and provided the hotline number to more than 7,100 online filers.

    Industry observers note that “The FTC has been on the front lines of tackling fraud for more than a century,” mentioned FTC Chairman and Anti-Fraud Task Force Vice Chairman Andrew N. Ferguson. “Thanks to President Trump’s comprehensive, government-wide approach to stopping fraud, the Trump FTC has returned almost $3 billion to American consumers who have been harmed by fraud and deception. The Trump Administration’s message to the bad actors who lie, cheat and steal to defraud Americans out of their hard-earned money is clear: you are living on borrowed time. The FTC is proud to work alongside its federal partners to protect Americans from scammers, whether the crooks are here at home or abroad.”.

    Securities and Exchange Commission.

    Since March 2026, the SEC has filed enforcement actions against 39 entities for allegedly filing false Forms ADV to create the appearance of legitimate U.S. investment advisers and lure retail investors and charged multiple entities with fraud in connection with so-called investment confidence scams that feigned SEC compliance while misappropriating more than $15 million from investors through online platforms. In the last year, the SEC also charged three purported crypto asset trading platforms and four investment clubs with allegedly defrauding retail investors of more than $14 million through an online investment-confidence scam. The SEC charged BG Wealth Sharing Ltd and DSJ Exchange Pty Ltd with an alleged investment fraud scheme that raised more than $130 million from tens of thousands of retail investors across the U.S. and abroad. The SEC has issued investor alerts warning investors that fraudsters may use social media platforms and messaging apps or claim to be officially registered with the SEC to lure investors into scams. The SEC also encourages investors to visit Investor.gov to verify the background of individuals offering investment opportunities.

    “Advances in technology have lowered the barriers to entry for fraudsters, making it easier to reach potential victims and making fraudulent schemes appear more legitimate,” noted David Woodcock, Director of the SEC's Division of Enforcement. “The technology may be latest, but the frauds are familiar. We will continue working with our law enforcement partners to target these schemes and hold those responsible accountable.”.

    Federal Communications Commission.

    On Nov. 19, the FCC approved a upcoming rule to allow federal and state prisons and jails to use jamming technology to block calls from illegal contraband cell phones that can be used to coordinate outside illegal activity, including the jury duty scams described above as well as scams explicitly targeting U.S. veterans. The FCC has also taken concrete actions to target scammers and illegal robocallers. The FCC has stopped nearly 300 million illegal robocalls, saving Americans at least $38 million through enforcement and reforms that led to the blocking of more than 1,400 providers and 296 million illegal robocalls. This includes removing from networks voice providers who unlawfully transmitted illegal scammer calls impersonating government agencies, internet service providers, banks, and major retailers. The FCC has published step-by-step guides that enable consumers to turn on blocking and filtering tools specific to devices and carriers.

    “President Trump has put restoring law and order and ensuring the safety of law-abiding Americans at the top of his agenda and that includes stopping scammers. For years, hundreds of thousands of contraband cellphones have entered our prisons allowing offenders to perpetrate scams on ordinary Americans including veteran Jared Johns who took his life after inmates extorted and threatened him. By allowing jamming in prisons for the first time, we’re taking an aggressive, but responsible approach to eliminate inmates access to contraband phones," remarked Chairman Carr. “The FCC continues to increase our work to crack down on scammers and protect consumers. We’ve taken extensive measures to strengthen consumers’ ability to revoke consent and stop unwanted calls including empowering consumers with instructions to block scam calls and texts, cutting off voices service providers from our networks after non-compliance and further incentivizing providers to block illegal calls so they never get to your phone in the first place.”.

    Sources indicate that an indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

    Latest Update: The Supreme Court and profanity

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2224 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • on October 30, 1973, John Douglas was driving with his 15-year-old son when he heard a litany of profanity come over the radio.
    • Industry observers note that the station later said it had chosen Carlin’s routine because it was an “incisive satirical view of the subject under discussion,” in the style of other great satirists like Mark Twain or Mort Sahl.
    • Recent findings suggest that before playing the routine, the host had warned that it included language some listeners might find offensive and suggested they return in 15 minutes if they were inclined toward offense.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Around 2 p.m. on October 30, 1973, John Douglas was driving with his 15-year-old son when he heard a litany of profanity come over the radio. New York’s WBAI, a nonprofit radio station, was airing a program on modern attitudes toward language. Near the end, the station played George Carlin’s “Filthy Words” routine, which begins with the comedian saying he’d been thinking about “the words you couldn’t say on the public airwaves; the ones you definitely wouldn’t say, ever.” He went on to repeat those words several times, contrasting them with words like “bastards,” “hell,” and “damn,” which were mostly acceptable, and showing how even some of his list of seven were perfectly fine in other contexts. His point was to show the absurdity of profanity.

    Industry observers note that the station later said it had chosen Carlin’s routine because it was an “incisive satirical view of the subject under discussion,” in the style of other great satirists like Mark Twain or Mort Sahl. Carlin, the station explained, was doing more than “mouthing obscenities.” He was “using words to satirize as harmless and essentially silly our attitudes towards those words.”.

    Recent findings suggest that before playing the routine, the host had warned that it included language some listeners might find offensive and suggested they return in 15 minutes if they were inclined toward offense. But about a month later, John Douglas complained to the Federal Communications Commission about the transmission which he remarked was “garbage” and had been broadcast in the presence of his “young son.” He was the only listener to do so. A member of Morality in Media who frequently listened to the station to “see how far” they’d go, Douglas later acknowledged that he had laughed out loud at the bit but “did not appreciate WBIA’s ‘smart-alecky’ on-air provocations.”.

    Industry observers note that the previous year, Carlin had been arrested after performing an earlier version of the same routine, but a judge threw out the charge. This time, the FCC found the broadcast “indecent,” and put its order in the station’s license file.

    That order ended up before the Supreme Court.

    Early in its order, the FCC acknowledged that Congress had forbade it from censoring broadcasts. But Congress had also prohibited the broadcast of “obscene, indecent, or profane” language, and the Commission thought Carlin’s broadcast fit the bill. In the FCC’s view, the ban on “indecent” language covered not just obscenity, but also patently offensive language when there was a reasonable risk of children listening. Late at night, when children were unlikely to be listening, the same material might be okay if it appeared in a work of serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value.

    Two commissioners thought even that was too permissive. Charlotte Reid believed “this language to be totally inappropriate for broadcast at anytime” and thought the commission’s standard did “not go far enough.” Commissioner James Quello took much the same view. “Garbage is garbage,” he wrote, whether children were listening or not.

    Industry observers note that the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, however, set aside the order in a 2-1 vote, with one judge believing it violated the statutory ban on censorship and the other saying it violated the First Amendment. The FCC appealed to the Supreme Court.

    In a recent development, at oral argument, which was held in April of 1978, several justices made their distaste for Carlin’s bit plain. When Pacifica’s lawyer stressed that the station had warned listeners beforehand and aired the monologue as part of an educational program about language, Chief Justice Warren Burger incredulously asked, “This is educational in your view?” And when counsel defended the material’s artistic value, Justice Thurgood Marshall responded, “Well, I’m not an expert, but if that’s artistic, deliver me.” Justice William Rehnquist, for his part, tested the limits of Pacifica’s position with a hypothetical involving a single four-letter word repeated for an hour. Would the FCC be powerless to prohibit that? Justice John Paul Stevens, however, seemed troubled by the potential reach of the FCC’s position, given that the prohibition on indecency could be enforced through criminal law.

    One striking exchange concerned the Justice Department’s position to argue separately, and more narrowly, than the FCC. The solicitor general’s office urged that the First Amendment prevented the government from barring particular words outright for a substantial part of the day without regard to context, even if the FCC could constitutionally regulate “indecency” to some extent. Rehnquist sharply asked why the Justice Department was arguing against the FCC, what interest it had in seeking a narrow construction of an act of Congress, and whether the solicitor general, as the government’s lawyer, could ever argue that an act of Congress was unconstitutional.

    Industry observers note that justice Lewis Powell also pressed the DOJ on the reasons behind its departure from the FCC, noting that the DOJ had supported the FCC in the court below. “That is true, and that is an embarrassment to us,” Deputy Solicitor General Louis Claiborne acknowledged, suggesting it was because the matter had been handled there by the Antitrust Division rather than the Criminal Division. Another explanation, which he did not mention, was that the administration had changed.

    Recent findings suggest that the court ultimately ruled 5-4 that the FCC could constitutionally treat this broadcast as “indecent” under the governing statute, and that the government could constitutionally prohibit indecency even though it fell short of legal obscenity. Stevens wrote for Burger, Justice Harry Blackmun, Powell, and Rehnquist, having apparently struggled with the case and flip-flopped before settling against Pacifica. The Commission had treated the piece as a nuisance, and, as the court had observed in Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co., a nuisance could be as simple as “a pig in the parlor instead of the barnyard.” He concluded that “when the Commission finds that a pig has entered the parlor, the exercise of its regulatory power does not depend on proof that the pig is obscene.” Though the holding expanded the government’s power to regulate speech, Stevens emphasized broadcasting’s pervasive presence in the home and its accessibility to children, the fact the piece was broadcast during the daytime, and the narrowness of the holding. He did not address late night broadcasts or the “occasional expletive.”.

    In a recent development, stevens had only three votes for some parts of his opinion. Powell, joined by Blackmun, wrote separately to object to Stevens’ suggestion that the level of protection that speech receives should depend on a judge’s perception of that speech’s value. For them, the combination of repeated, patently offensive language, an afternoon broadcast, and children’s ready access was enough to resolve the case. Powell also addressed the concern that the decision could end up “reduc[ing] the adult population . . . to [hearing] only what is fit for children”: adults could buy tapes or hear the same words at theaters.

    It has been revealed that justice Potter Stewart dissented, joined by Justices William Brennan, Byron White, and Marshall. Stewart would have resolved the case on statutory grounds. He read “indecent” to reach only obscene material, and everyone agreed that Carlin’s monologue fell outside that category. His opinion recalled his concurrence in Jacobellis v. Ohio, where he voted to overturn an obscenity conviction for showing a French film with an explicit love scene. Stewart understood obscenity narrowly, but declined to define it, famously observing in that case, “I know it when I see it, and the motion picture involved in this case is not that.”.

    Brennan wrote a separate dissent, joined by Marshall, that went further. He agreed with Stewart on the statute and said he would ordinarily refrain from addressing the constitutional question, but he found “the Court’s misapplication of fundamental First Amendment principles so patent, and its attempt to impose its notions of propriety on the whole of the American people so misguided,” that he was “unable to remain silent.”.

    Brennan disputed the analogy between a radio broadcast and an intrusion into the home. Listeners voluntarily turn on the radio, and they can voluntarily turn it off. In perhaps his sharpest passage, he wrote:.

    According to recent reports, brennan also questioned the majority’s reliance on protecting children. He read the court’s precedents as allowing the government to shield children from material that was obscene as to them. In his view, Carlin’s routine fell outside that category. Keeping it off the radio during the afternoon cut off access for adults as well as children. And while the majority had invoked parents’ right to raise their children as they saw fit, Brennan thought the FCC had somewhat ironically made the choice for them.

    It has been revealed that finally, he remained unconvinced that the court’s reasoning would reach only cases like Carlin’s. Among the things it could sweep in were “literary works, novels, poems, and plays by the likes of Shakespeare, Joyce, Hemingway, Ben Jonson, Henry Fielding, Robert Burns, and Chaucer,” “a good deal of political speech, such as the Nixon tapes,” and even portions of the Bible. In his view, the public, and not the court, should have the power to weed out “worthless and offensive” speech in a marketplace “unsullied by the censor’s hand.”.

    Recent findings suggest that brennan and Marshall had joined together in another Supreme Court opinion involving the F-word. In Cohen v. California, they joined Justice John Harlan II’s opinion protecting the right to wear a jacket emblazoned with “Fuck the Draft.” Stewart joined it too (not surprisingly, Burger and Blackmun dissented). Brennan brought Cohen straight into his Pacifica dissent; as he made clear, changing the words can change what the speaker communicates, something that applies especially well to Carlin because the taboo words were themselves the subject of the routine. And Brennan thought telling listeners to buy a record or pay to see Carlin live missed what it meant to hear the routine on the radio.

    In closing, Brennan wrote that the majority had only “confirm[ed] Carlin’s prescience as a social commentator.” (It was interesting that Marshall, who sounded distinctly unimpressed by the claim of artistic merit at oral argument, joined him, perhaps especially here.) As Brennan pointed out, Carlin had made fun of the rules about which words you could say on the air, and the court had exemplified the very attitude he was satirizing. To top it all off: Appended to the opinion is the transcript of Carlin’s routine, giving his “indecent” words a permanent home in the U.S. Reports.

    In a recent development, at the 2002 Billboard Music Awards on Fox, Cher dispatched the critics who’d spent decades predicting her downfall with “So f*** ’em.” At the 2003 awards, Nicole Richie asked whether anyone had tried getting cow manure out of a Prada purse, then used the F-word to describe how hard it was. The next year, after Bono called U2’s Golden Globe win “really, really f***ing brilliant,” the FCC revealed that even a single expletive could be indecent, and it later applied that approach to the two earlier Fox broadcasts.

    In 2009, the Supreme Court took up the dispute in FCC v. Fox Television Stations. Writing for a 5-4 majority, Justice Antonin Scalia held that the FCC had adequately explained its change in policy under the Administrative Procedure Act, leaving the First Amendment question open. Justice Clarence Thomas joined the majority but wrote separately to question Pacifica’s holding. On remand, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit struck down the policy as unconstitutionally vague.

    The case returned to the Supreme Court in 2012 and all eight participating justices agreed on the result (Justice Sonia Sotomayor recused herself). Justice Anthony Kennedy’s opinion held that the FCC had failed to give Fox fair notice that fleeting expletives could trigger an indecency finding, but once again left both Pacifica and the First Amendment question open. Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg wrote separately to say that Pacifica was wrong from the start and deserved reconsideration. But while the court has had several cases involving curse words since, it has yet to take up the question directly.

    Sources indicate that in 2004, the FCC dismissed complaints related to the airing of Saving Private Ryan on the basis that the film’s curse words helped convey the soldiers’ experience. But just two years later, it slapped a station with $15,000 in fines for airing a Martin Scorsese documentary about Blues music that contained profanity. In 2020, the FCC received over 1,300 complaints about Jennifer Lopez and Shakira’s halftime show, though it never took any action against the network. And in February 2026, FCC requested transcripts of Bad Bunny’s Superbowl halftime performance before ultimately finding no violation.

    Half a century after Carlin’s seven dirty words, the FCC’s continued and seemingly arbitrary application of its indecency laws demonstrates the prescience of Brennan’s dissent and the need to finally answer the question of whether the Constitution prohibits the “dominant culture” from trying to force “groups who do not share its mores to conform to its way of acting, thinking, and speaking.”.

    Anastasia Boden is a Senior Attorney at the Pacific Legal Foundation, where she brings civil rights lawsuits that advance the Constitution’s promises of equality and economic opportunity.

    • The jury delivered its verdict Tuesday following an 11-week trial in which prosecutors argued that the company committed “crime after crime” to build its empire, Law.com reports.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    After four days of deliberations, a federal jury convicted the Chinese telecommunications giant Huawei of conspiring to steal trade secrets and evade U.S. sanctions on Iran. (Photo from Shutterstock).

    In a recent development, after four days of deliberations, a federal jury convicted the Chinese telecommunications giant Huawei of conspiring to steal trade secrets and evade U.S. sanctions on Iran.

    The jury delivered its verdict Tuesday following an 11-week trial in which prosecutors argued that the company committed “crime after crime” to build its empire, Law.com reports.

    Industry observers note that the tech giant was found guilty of conspiring to steal trade secrets, commit wire and bank fraud, violate U.S. sanctions and launder money, as well as multiple fraud charges. In all, Huawei was found guilty of 10 out of the 12 counts tried by prosecutors at the U.S. attorney’s office for the Eastern District of Upcoming York.

    “Few crimes are as serious as Huawei’s decades-long pattern of endangering U.S. national security, violating the sanctity of U.S. commerce, and impeding the enforcement of U.S. laws,” U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella said in a statement. “Today’s verdict is a step towards accountability for Huawei’s criminal activities, which includes yearslong collaboration with sanctioned entities in Iran, repeated lies to banks, and blatant thefts from U.S. technology companies.”.

    Industry observers note that jurors, however, rejected the lead racketeering conspiracy charge, as well as one count of conspiring to obstruct justice. Defense attorney Brian Heberlig claimed that as a victory.

    “It’s hard not to have profoundly mixed emotions from the verdict we just heard, but the single lead charge that was brought by the United States government against Huawei was the RICO charge, a charge that alleged that the firm was corrupt from top to bottom,” Heberlig stated in a press conference immediately after the verdict was announced.

    #227636. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson and the arc of the law

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (266 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson and the arc of the law

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (266 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In September, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson received an award named after the late Justice William Brennan, a liberal lion.
    • Since joining the court in the summer of 2022, Jackson has sought to promote her understanding of that view.
    • Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    In September, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson received an award named after the late Justice William Brennan, a liberal lion. In her acceptance speech, Jackson discussed Brennan’s role as the Supreme Court became more conservative, noting that he “believed that even his dissents could make a difference and remind the nation that the pursuit of equal justice under law is an ongoing effort.” Jackson indicated that she agreed with that idea, telling the audience that she saw “dissent[s] as more than just a disagreement with the outcome of a case, I see them as an expression of faith in the future and a demonstration of hope.” As she put it, “However desolate the moment feels, we who write for a future age have hope that the noble and collective work of bending the long arc of the law toward justice will continue.”.

    Since joining the court in the summer of 2022, Jackson has sought to promote her understanding of that view. Although she has been consistently part of the court’s liberal bloc, even among the three Democratic appointees she has forged a unique role. As her invocation of Brennan suggests, it often appears that her goal is not simply to express disagreement with the majority, but to offer an alternative vision and to speak to the public directly – even if she does so without the support of her fellow liberals.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    In an unprecedented move, a U.S. federal appeals court has instituted a rule requiring mandatory human review of all court filings that use artificial intelligence.

    According to recent reports, the 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at Denver posted a upcoming rule Friday stipulating attorneys and pro see parties certify human verification of all cited authorities and quotations, Law360 reports.

    It has been revealed that at the start of next year, the 10th Circuit can address violations by waiving the affected glitch, striking a noncompliant document or affirming or dismissing an appeal. The judge may also impose monetary sanctions or demand coverage of some of the opponent’s attorney fees.

    In a recent development, four years after generative AI debuted on a mass scale, many fake citations have been discovered in court filings resulting from large language models sometimes producing false information or hallucinations, according to Law360. French data consultant Damien Charlotin found that court cases involving hallucinated case citations worldwide have decreased this year, which he attributes to hallucination awareness and LLM improvements.

    #227629. Tech Report: The Second Amendment and an "unusually dangerous" approach to dicta

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1826 w)

    Tech Report: The Second Amendment and an "unusually dangerous" approach to dicta

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1826 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.
    • On November 10, The New York Times published an article suggesting that a major piece of the Supreme Court’s Second Amendment jurisprudence is premised on a misquote by the late Justice Antonin Scalia in his 2008 majority opinion in D.C v.
    • According to the Times piece, “[t]he consequences of Justice Scalia’s use of ‘and’ rather than ‘or’ have been profound”: “Since all guns are dangerous, courts have had to focus instead on determining whether a type of firearm is unusual, often parsing marketing data and consumer surveys to gauge a weapon’s popularity.” Presumably, if Scalia had used the phrase “dangerous or unusual,” it would be easier for legislatures to ban even certain commonly owned firearms because dangerousness alone would be sufficient to bring a category of weapons outside the amendment’s protective sphere.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.

    On November 10, The New York Times published an article suggesting that a major piece of the Supreme Court’s Second Amendment jurisprudence is premised on a misquote by the late Justice Antonin Scalia in his 2008 majority opinion in D.C v. Heller, in which the court held that there was an individual right to possess firearms. The essence of the piece is that Scalia used the phrase “dangerous and unusual” to describe those weapons not protected by the right to keep and bear arms, attributing this terminology primarily (or perhaps solely) to the 18th century British jurist William Blackstone. Yet Blackstone’s writings instead use the phrase “dangerous or unusual.”.

    According to the Times piece, “[t]he consequences of Justice Scalia’s use of ‘and’ rather than ‘or’ have been profound”: “Since all guns are dangerous, courts have had to focus instead on determining whether a type of firearm is unusual, often parsing marketing data and consumer surveys to gauge a weapon’s popularity.” Presumably, if Scalia had used the phrase “dangerous or unusual,” it would be easier for legislatures to ban even certain commonly owned firearms because dangerousness alone would be sufficient to bring a category of weapons outside the amendment’s protective sphere.

    Sources indicate that the Times story has reverberated quickly, with strong backlash from conservative lawyers and scholars. Such disagreements have focused largely on the specific citation Scalia used. Law professor Jonathan Adler, for example, has argued that the citation to Blackstone was one among many, and additional sources that Scalia cited used the “and” formulation. Others have responded that Scalia was anything but sloppy, which would be especially true when it came to such an influential and key source.

    Recent findings suggest that both sides, though, seem to be burying the lede. In my view, this is a story not about historical errors or the nuances of legal citation. Rather, it is about how judicial dicta that was never intended to lay down broad, permanent rules has taken on a life of its own, and how other justices on the Supreme Court subsequently canonized Scalia’s stray language by turning it into a “test” that would govern any number of future cases – when it’s not at all clear Scalia ever contemplated this or would have endorsed any such thing.

    As most law students and lawyers are well aware, the holding-dicta distinction is deeply rooted in American jurisprudence: generally speaking, the holding is the analysis necessary to resolve the actual case before the court, and everything else in an opinion is dicta (this comes from the Latin phrase “obiter dictum,” or “stated in passing”). Fundamental to that distinction is that dicta, while it may be persuasive, is not precedential. As Chief Justice John Marshall wrote in 1821, the reason for not deferring blindly to dicta is “obvious”:.

    The late Judge Richard Posner once similarly emphasized the risk that dicta “can be misleading if carelessly lifted from the case-specific contexts in which they were originally uttered … That is why courts in assessing the binding effect of previous decisions distinguish between the dicta, which are the inessential parts of the opinion, and the holding.” Circuits vary in their approach to Supreme Court dicta, generally deferring more heavily to such language when they find it thoroughly considered or supported, but the court is, of course, never bound by its own dicta.

    According to recent reports, in fact, Scalia himself was no fan of relying heavily on dicta from prior Supreme Court decisions. In a 1993 opinion, he criticized a group of dissenting justices by noting that their position found “support, if at all, only in the dicta of this Court’s opinions.” This was, in Scalia’s view, as good as no support at all. Indeed, Scalia rejected reliance on “drive-by … rulings” not fully considered by the issuing court, even if not purely dicta. In his 2015 decision for the court in Kerry v. Din, Scalia excoriated a proposition advanced in a dissenting opinion as resting solely on “dictum in a footnote” and then observed that “[t]he footnoted dictum that Justice Breyer proposes to elevate to constitutional law is a dangerous doctrine.” He further joined opinions that rejected prior dicta as unprincipled, especially when greater investigation revealed reasons for caution.

    According to recent reports, scalia’s position was nuanced – for example, he once joined a dissent by Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg that endorsed reliance on certain dictum as persuasive – yet a cautious approach to dicta is consistent with his broader judicial philosophy as well. He was at times willing to jettison even precedential decisions squarely applicable to the case at hand when those decisions were contrary to original public meaning. Unconsidered dicta, presumably, would then be far lower in the pecking order.

    It has been revealed that returning to Heller and the phrase at problem, it’s hard to argue that the “dangerous and unusual” passage from Heller is anything but dicta. The issue in Heller was whether a Washington, D.C. ordinance “generally prohibit[ing] the possession of handguns” violated the Second Amendment, or if there was an individual right to keep arms for one’s self-defense. Scalia’s majority opinion answered in the affirmative, as “the American people have considered the handgun to be the quintessential self-defense weapon.” D.C. never argued that handguns were entirely exempt from protection because they were especially dangerous. The question of dangerous and/or unusual weapons was not at issue in the case; accordingly, it wasn’t thoroughly investigated through the adversarial process.

    Rather, after canvassing the historical evidence and concluding it supported an individual-rights view of the Second Amendment, Scalia turned to the nature of the right he had just explicated. In three short paragraphs not necessary to the holding, he explained why the amendment did not authorize gun keeping-and-carrying by anyone in any circumstance; rather history revealed limitations on the right, such as “the carrying of ‘dangerous and unusual weapons.’”.

    Whatever the purpose of this section – Justice John Paul Stevens later suggested the language was proposed by Justice Anthony Kennedy (the crucial fifth vote in Heller) in exchange for joining the majority – it was far from necessary to resolve the case at hand.

    Sources indicate that so how did such dicta become relevant? In the 2016 case Caetano v. Massachusetts, decided after Scalia had passed away, the justices unanimously overturned a Massachusetts Supreme Court decision upholding that state’s ban on stun guns in a criminal prosecution of a woman who used this weapon to defend herself from an abusive ex-boyfriend. Justice Samuel Alito issued a concurring opinion (joined by Justice Clarence Thomas) that performed an interesting maneuver. Seizing on the fact that the per curiam opinion in that case referenced Scalia’s “dangerous and unusual” formulation, Alito turned Scalia’s language into a doctrinal test: “As the per curiam opinion recognizes, this is a conjunctive test: A weapon may not be banned unless it is both dangerous and unusual.” But the per curiam had done no such thing; rather, that opinion simply cited the passage in Heller as referring to one limitation on the right to keep and bear arms. And the per curiam remarked that the lower court in that case had faltered by concluding that any weapon not in common use in 1791 was per se unusual, not by failing to use a conjunctive test.

    (Ironically, Alito has his own well-publicized objections to giving past Supreme Court dicta undue veneration – his opinion for the court in Dobbs heavily suggested that Roe’s viability framework was entitled to less weight in the stare decisis analysis because it was initially mere dicta, “the Court’s own brainchild [for which n]either party advocated.”).

    From there, the “dangerous and unusual” language took on a life of its own. In 2022’s Latest York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen, in which the court struck down New York’s concealed-carry law, the majority set forth a test for Second Amendment constitutionality privileging historical evidence above all else. At the first step of that test, a court determines whether the conduct at matter is protected by the right to keep and bear arms, which is where the exclusion of dangerous and/or unusual weapons becomes relevant. If the banned weapon is not protected by the Second Amendment (for, say, being “dangerous and unusual”), a constitutional challenge is dead on arrival. If, on the other hand, the plaintiff can show the weapons are protected, then the burden switches to the government to provide historical evidence to support its regulation. (The consequences may be even greater, as some have argued that “usualness” (or “common use”) conclusively establishes not only threshold protection for the weapon but also that any legislative ban is ahistorical and thus unconstitutional.).

    According to recent reports, this test has divided the judiciary in recent years. For example, a Massachusetts federal judge evaluating a challenge to that state’s AR-15 ban recognized the apparent disconnect between Heller and Blackstone but nevertheless noted that “the Supreme Court has expressly stated . . .that the relevant tradition is one of regulating ‘dangerous and unusual weapons.’” The Massachusetts judge found these weapons were not in “common use,” and, in any event, a historical tradition of responding to technological advances by regulating specific weapons supported the ban. By contrast, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit interpreted Scalia’s language to signal that widespread ownership of AR-15s and large-capacity magazines meant any legislative attempt to ban them was unconstitutional. The “dangerous and unusual” framework has led other judges on a search for ownership statistics and sales data to assess a weapon’s popularity, triggering sharp debate over whether a test that ultimately turns on commonality is even workable.

    This is particularly relevant since the court is right now preparing to hear oral argument in Viramontes v. Cook County, a Second Amendment challenge to state and local bans on AR-15s, on December 2. While the recent attention to Scalia’s citation may trigger discussion at oral argument, most justices are now likely to treat “dangerous and unusual” as an established standard and ownership statistics as definitive proof that AR-15s are not unusual and thus protected. Absent from this, however, will be the fact that this standard did not emerge from any well-reasoned, litigation-tested analysis making it deserve deference in the first place – especially under Scalia’s own approach to judging.

    The debate over Scalia’s Blackstone citation, then, has obscured a more important problem: the Supreme Court’s decision to treat its past dicta as doctrine that can settle the outcome of cases on which the court has never passed.

    Andrew Willinger is an Assistant Professor at Georgia State University College of Law, where he teaches constitutional law and civil procedure.
